title: BEACON: Language-Conditioned Navigation Affordance Prediction under Occlusion
abstract: Language-conditioned local navigation requires a robot to infer a nearby traversable target location from its current observation and an open-vocabulary, relational instruction. Existing vision-language spatial grounding methods usually rely on vision–language models (VLMs) to reason in image space, producing 2D predictions tied to visible pixels. As a result, they struggle to infer target locations in occluded regions, typically caused by furniture or moving humans. To address this issue, we propose BEACON, which predicts an ego-centric Bird’s-Eye View (BEV) affordance heatmap over a bounded local region including occluded areas. Given an instruction and surround-view RGB-D observations from four directions around the robot, BEACON predicts the BEV heatmap by injecting spatial cues into a VLM and fusing the VLM’s output with depth-derived BEV features. Using an occlusion-aware dataset built in the Habitat simulator, we conduct detailed experimental analysis to validate both our BEV space formulation and the design choices of each module. Our method improves the accuracy averaged across geodesic thresholds by 22.74 percentage points over the state-of-the-art image-space baseline on the validation subset with occluded target locations.

title: Explore Like Humans: Autonomous Exploration with Online SG-Memo Construction for Embodied Agents
abstract: Constructing structured spatial memory is essential for enabling long-horizon reasoning in complex embodied navigation tasks. Current memory construction predominantly relies on a decoupled, two-stage paradigm: agents first aggregate environmental data through exploration, followed by the offline reconstruction of spatial memory. However, this post-hoc and geometry-centric approach precludes agents from leveraging high-level semantic intelligence, often causing them to overlook navigationally critical landmarks (e.g., doorways and staircases) that serve as fundamental semantic anchors in human cognitive maps. To bridge this gap, we propose ABot-Explorer, a novel active exploration framework that unifies memory construction and exploration into an online, RGB-only process. At its core, ABot-Explorer leverages Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to distill Semantic Navigational Affordances (SNA), which act as cognitive-aligned anchors to guide the agent’s movement. By dynamically integrating these SNAs into a hierarchical SG-Memo, ABot-Explorer mirrors human-like exploratory logic by prioritizing structural transit nodes to facilitate efficient coverage. To support this framework, we contribute a large-scale dataset extending InteriorGS with SNA and SG-Memo annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that ABot-Explorer significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both exploration efficiency and environment coverage, while the resulting SG-Memo is shown to effectively support diverse downstream tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/amap-cvlab/ABot-Explorer.

title: SparseNav: Efficient Zero-Shot Object-Goal Navigation with Multi-Layer Sparse Semantic Mapping
abstract: Zero-shot object-goal navigation presents a significant challenge for autonomous robots operating in novel environments. While recent advances in vision-language models have enabled impressive generalization capabilities, existing approaches suffer from either excessive computational overhead from frequent model inference or suboptimal navigation efficiency due to limited spatial reasoning. In this paper, we present SparseNav, a novel zero-shot object-goal navigation framework that addresses these limitations through three key innovations. First, we introduce a multi-layer sparse semantic mapping strategy that efficiently encodes object and scene information by extracting only semantically dense image regions and employing non-uniform height stratification. Second, we propose a dynamic scoring mechanism that adaptively balances scene priors and object beliefs throughout the navigation episode, implementing an effective explore-first, exploit-later strategy. Third, we design a verify-and-blacklist mechanism to handle the inherent unreliability of open-vocabulary object detectors in edge scenarios. Extensive experiments on the HM3D benchmark demonstrate that SparseNav achieves a 53.58% success rate and 22.49% SPL on single-floor episodes, outperforming most existing zero-shot methods while maintaining real-time operation suitable for resource-constrained platforms. Real-world deployment on a Jetson AGX Orin further validates the practical applicability of our approach.

title: Stairway to Success: An Online Floor-Aware Zero-Shot Object-Goal Navigation Framework Via LLM-Driven Coarse-To-Fine Exploration
abstract: Deployable service and delivery robots struggle to navigate multi-floor buildings to reach object goals, as existing systems fail due to single-floor assumptions and requirements for offline, globally consistent maps. Multi-floor environments pose unique challenges including cross-floor transitions and vertical spatial reasoning,especially navigating unknown buildings. Object-Goal Navigation benchmarks like HM3D and MP3D also capture this multi-floor reality, yet current methods lack support for online, floor-aware navigation. To bridge this gap, we propose ASCENT, an online framework for Zero-Shot Object-Goal Navigation that enables robots to operate without pre-built maps or retraining on new object categories. It introduces: (1) a Multi-Floor Abstraction module that dynamically constructs hierarchical representations with stair-aware obstacle mapping and cross-floor topology modeling, and (2) a Coarse-to-Fine Reasoning module that combines frontier ranking with LLM-driven contextual analysis for multi-floor navigation decisions. We evaluate on HM3D and MP3D benchmarks, outperforming state-of-the-art zero-shot approaches, and demonstrate real-world deployment on a quadruped robot. Code will be released.

title: Where Did I Leave My Glasses? Open-Vocabulary Semantic Exploration in Real-World Semi-Static Environments
abstract: Robots deployed in real-world environments, such as homes, must not only navigate safely but also understand their surroundings and adapt to changes in the environment. To perform tasks efficiently, they must build and maintain a semantic map that accurately reflects the current state of the environment. Existing research on semantic exploration largely focuses on static scenes without persistent object-level instance tracking. In this work, we propose an open-vocabulary, semantic exploration system for semi-static environments. Our system maintains a consistent map by building a probabilistic model of object instance stationarity, systematically tracking semi-static changes, and actively exploring areas that have not been visited for an extended period. In addition to active map maintenance, our approach leverages the map’s semantic richness with large language model (LLM)-based reasoning for open-vocabulary object-goal navigation. This enables the robot to search more efficiently by prioritizing contextually relevant areas. We evaluate our approach in 60 simulation tasks and on public mapping datasets against state-of-the-art baselines, and show real-world transferability in three real-world scenes. In dynamic scenes, our method achieves an average 25% increase in success weighted by path length (SPL), and an average 26.5% improvement in change detection F1 score. Our system detects 95% of map changes on average, improving efficiency by more than 29% as compared to random and patrol baselines. A video of our work can be found at http://tiny.cc/sem-explor-semi-static.

title: D3D-GEN: Robot-Aware Domain-Grounded Interactive 3D World Generation for Social Robotics
abstract: Training and validation of Embodied AI for social navigation critically depends on realistic simulation environments, yet many current approaches fail to find a balance between realism and simulability. We propose D3D-GEN, a novel world generation system that combines a domain agent with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in that domain. Our system enables users to rapidly generate domain-grounded, fully interactive 3D worlds by automating both the collection of domain knowledge and the synthesis of realistic floorplans and object placements, without dependence on any fixed 3D model database. Given a domain description prompt, the research agent collects publicly accessible domain-specific data and constructs a persistent domain database. Using this database, our RAG pipeline generates plausible floorplans and object placements by dynamically querying a user-provided semantic database, which can be easily extended or modified. The output is a fully interactive 3D world loadable by the popular simulators Isaac Sim and Gazebo. With our approach, we have built databases for several common domains (indoor residential, hospital, office) and generated dozens of distinct, plausible simulation environments for each domain. We present D3D-GEN with a local web frontend that facilitates rapid, interactive world generation for robot simulation.

title: How VLAs (Really) Work in Open-World Environments
abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have been extensively used in robotics applications, achieving great success in various manipulation problems. More recently, VLAs have been used in long-horizon tasks and evaluated on benchmarks, such as BEHAVIOR1K (B1K), for solving complex household chores. The common metric for measuring progress in such benchmarks is success rate or partial score based on satisfaction of progress-agnostic criteria, meaning only the final states of the objects are considered, regardless of the events that lead to such states. In this paper, we argue that using such evaluation protocols say little about safety aspects of operation and can potentially exaggerate reported performance, undermining core challenges for future real-world deployment. To this end, we conduct a thorough analysis of state-of-the-art models on the B1K Challenge and evaluate policies in terms of robustness via reproducibility and consistency of performance, safety aspects of policies operations, task awareness, and key elements leading to the incompletion of tasks. We then propose evaluation protocols to capture safety violations to better measure the true performance of the policies in more complex and interactive scenarios. At the end, we discuss the limitations of the existing VLAs and motivate future research.

title: SafeLoop: Risk-Aware Rollback for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models are promising for general-purpose manipulation, but long-horizon execution remains fragile. Small state-estimation or control errors can lead to irreversible failures (e.g., collisions and object drops). Avoiding these risks requires a proactive safety mechanism capable of anticipating hazards. In this paper, we introduce SafeLoop, a non-invasive external wrapper that adds hazard prediction and rollback-based recovery to a VLA model without changing its parameters. SafeLoop trains a risk predictor from vision and proprioception to output four values: the probability and time-to-hazard for body collisions and for object failures. A lightweight controller then chooses one of three actions based on the predicted risk: continue execution (noop), save a safety checkpoint (record), or retreat in joint space (rollback). Rollback moves the robot back to a recent safe waypoint and queries the base policy again, which may yield an alternative continuation. Across 24 LIBERO tasks (16 random seeds each) and three real-robot tasks (25 rollouts each), SafeLoop achieves a stronger overall safety-success trade-off than alternative methods, reducing hazard cases by roughly 70% while preserving task success and the base-policy control rate. Project code is available at https://github.com/Loule0-0/SafeLoop/tree/release/safeloop.

title: Adaptive Embodied AI for Robust Environmental Monitoring in Field Robotics
abstract: Robotic autonomy in unstructured outdoor environments remains challenging due to uncertainty, sensor degradation, partial observability, and dynamic environmental variability. We present a closed-loop embodied AI framework for robust field robotics integrating multimodal perception, uncertaintyaware online adaptation, reinforcement learning (RL), and model predictive control (MPC). The proposed architecture consists of four tightly coupled modules: (i) an RGB-D perception encoder producing latent environmental representations, (ii) an uncertainty estimation module based on predictive entropy, (iii) an online self-supervised adaptation mechanism for representation refinement under distributional shifts, and (iv) a hybrid RL+MPC control stack in which RL generates nominal actions while MPC enforces safety and dynamic feasibility constraints. Experiments are conducted in NVIDIA Isaac Sim across randomized forest-navigation scenarios involving varying terrain slope, vegetation density, sensor noise, and partial occlusions. Compared with non-adaptive RL, MPC-only, and vision-only baselines, the proposed approach improves task success rate by 21% and reduces collision frequency by 35%. Ablation studies demonstrate that uncertainty-triggered adaptation and MPC safety filtering are both critical for robust autonomy in dynamic outdoor environments.

title: Desc++: Efficient Descriptor Enhancement for Data Association in Existing Visual SLAM Systems
abstract: Reliable visual data association is fundamental to visual SLAM (V-SLAM), yet the handcrafted descriptors used by most mature real-time systems degrade under illumination and viewpoint changes, while learned front-ends that address this weakness require replacing the entire pipeline and incur substantial computational overhead. We present Desc++, a lightweight descriptor enhancement module that jointly encodes descriptors and keypoint geometry, and aggregates spatial context through a parallel hybrid of attention-free global attention and geometry-aware Mamba sequential modeling over Z-order serialized keypoints, all in linear time. The enhanced descriptors retain the original dimensionality and matching interface, enabling plug-and-play integration into deployed systems. Desc++ outperforms the state-of-the-art enhancer on the HPatches benchmark. Integrated into four heterogeneous SLAM systems, it reduces trajectory error on the majority of EuRoC, KITTI, and Hilti 2023 sequences at only +5.3 ms additional front-end latency.

title: Cooperative Surveillance and Mapping using a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent System
abstract: Autonomously mapping unknown environments requires reconciling a fundamental trade-off between speed and detail: Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) offer high-resolution LiDAR sensing but navigate slowly and are prone to obstacle-induced blockages, while Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) survey terrain rapidly but lack ground-level resolution and cannot perceive beneath structures. This work introduces a Hierarchical-Cooperative SLAM (HC-SLAM) framework that unifies the broad situational awareness of a UAV coordinator with the fine-grained sensing of a swarm of UGV explorers, coordinated through a learned multi-agent policy rather than fixed heuristics. The system's agentic control layer uses Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) integrated with a Graph Neural Network (GNN), allowing agents to dynamically construct a communication graph in which agents are nodes and line-of-sight connections are edges. The UAV coordinator builds a coarse map via visual SLAM, identifies unexplored frontiers, and publishes goal coordinates; each UGV explorer receives these goals, fuses them with local sensor data through the GNN, and executes velocity commands via an actor-critic policy, continuously updating a fused global map. Policies were trained in a custom 2D Pygame environment wrapped in PettingZoo, featuring a vectorized 360-degree LiDAR array and reward shaping that incentivizes rapid target acquisition while penalizing collisions. Training over 5,000 episodes showed stable convergence, with cumulative rewards climbing from an initial -50 penalty to a +100 plateau. The trained policy roughly halved its steps-to-target by episode 4,000, and the cooperative GNN-MAPPO policy reached targets approximately 40% faster than a deterministic floodfill baseline. These results demonstrate that learned, graph-based multi-agent coordination can meaningfully outperform rule-based exploration in heterogeneous UGV-UAV teams. Future work will address real-time compute offloading to reduce network bottlenecks and extend physical testing beyond indoor environments toward unstructured, N-agent outdoor disaster-response scenarios.

title: Peristaltic Conduits with Stiff Skeletons and Compliant Skins
abstract: Although overhead power lines are less expensive to install than underground utilities, they are substantially more vulnerable to weather-related disruptions. Conventional underground installation methods, such as horizontal directional drilling (HDD), are costly, can disrupt surface infrastructure, and require specialized equipment, motivating the development of alternative installation approaches. We propose a bio-inspired concept in which electrical conduit is enclosed within a worm-like peristaltic robotic sleeve equipped with a drilling head, enabling simultaneous burrowing and conduit installation in a single operation. Because propulsion is distributed along the conduit rather than generated by a single drilling machine, such a system may reduce limitations associated with increasing drag during installation while potentially providing improved sensitivity to contact with buried infrastructure. As an initial step toward this vision, we designed, fabricated, simulated, and experimentally evaluated prototype worm-like robots capable of transporting conduit through an existing borehole. We also performed finite element structural analyses and geotechnical soil-interaction simulations to evaluate the mechanical performance and underground feasibility of the proposed system. These results establish the feasibility of peristaltic robotic conduit transport and represent an early step toward self-propelled underground conduit installation.

title: Correntropy-Based Adaptive Sensor Fusion on E2(3) for Robust USV Heading Estimation
abstract: This paper presents a novel sensor fusion method for adaptive and robust heading estimation of unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) based on Lie theory. Reliable heading information plays a critical role throughout the entire data association process for path following, mission planning, and multi-modal perception systems such as Radar, LiDAR, and cameras. However, real marine environments exhibit highly dynamic characteristics due to wind, waves, and currents, necessitating a robust heading estimation technique adaptive to such disturbances. The proposed method fuses attitude measurements from a dual-antenna Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and an Attitude Heading Reference System (AHRS). By formulating the state space on the Lie group SE2(3), the framework naturally handles the nonlinear geometry of attitude and motion. The key contribution is the introduction of a real-time sensor reliability assessment based on correntropy within the Lie theory framework, enabling dynamic evaluation of sensor trustworthiness under noise, bias, and data outages. These reliability weights are then used to adaptively adjust the fusion process. Furthermore, the filter dynamically switches measurement models according to sensor availability and reliability, ensuring robustness even during severe data dropouts. Extensive simulations and field experiments demonstrate that the proposed method, termed Adaptive Lie Filter (AdLF), outperforms conventional approaches, including linearized fusion filters and standalone GNSS or AHRS estimations. The proposed approach achieves high-accuracy heading tracking while maintaining stable convergence of internal state covariances under challenging environmental conditions.

title: Cable-Driven Soft-Legged Quadruped Robot: Design, Control, and Locomotion
abstract: Introduction & Design This poster presents the design, modelling, and control of an amphibious, cable-driven, soft-legged quadruped robot. Because the cable-driven actuation system requires no motors at the leg joints, it enables versatile locomotion on both land and water. Each leg is designed as a surface material in the shape of an arc. Motorized pulleys control the length of cables attached at two points (representing the ""knee"" and ""foot""), allowing compliant motion while maintaining controllability. Additionally, pool noodle attachments enable the robot to float. Trajectory Generation & Kinematics A core challenge was generating effective walking trajectories for the soft legs. While three initial trajectories were calculated based on leg geometry, a biologically inspired approach was adopted to improve realism. This method mapped foot trajectories from rigid-leg dog locomotion studies using joint angle equations: Shoulder joint: f(ϕ)=-0.3+sf[0.4 cos⁡ϕ+0.1 cos⁡(2ϕ)+0.6] Elbow joint: f(ϕ)=0.45+sf[0.3 cos⁡ϕ+1.1+0.2 cos⁡(2ϕ)+2.9] (Where ϕ represents the gait cycle index and sf is a scaling factor). To determine motor positions, cable lengths were calculated by solving the inverse kinematics of the soft mechanism. To resolve early issues with cable slacking and slipping under load, a collaborator's soft-leg model enabled workspace analysis by sampling maximum feasible cable lengths. Trimming the trajectory to fit within this workspace ensured consistent cable tension and smoother movement. Experimental Validation Terrestrial Locomotion: Tracking via ArUco markers and a camera verified that the robot can walk in a relatively straight line and execute left/right turns along an arc. Aquatic Locomotion: Because the walking gait provided insufficient propulsion in water, a dedicated swimming gait with larger leg excursions was introduced. Three swimming patterns were tested: 1) Sequential gait mirroring the walking pattern. 2) Front-and-rear gait (front legs move simultaneously, followed by rear), which proved most effective due to the larger force generated. 3) Synchronous gait (all four legs move simultaneously), which was least effective because leg retraction pushed the robot backward. Conclusion & Future Work This project demonstrates the feasibility of cable-driven soft quadrupeds for multi-environment operations by combining bio-inspired trajectories, workspace-constrained planning, and empirical testing. Future work will focus on weight reduction, advanced control algorithms, optimized leg materials, and navigating complex environments. This versatile platform holds strong potential for search-and-rescue, environmental monitoring, and amphibious exploration.

title: Multi-Sensor Fusion-based Situational Awareness for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships: Current Progress and Future Work
abstract: With advances in probabilistic inference, AI, and high-performance computing, autonomous navigation has made great strides. Yet, ships remain uniquely challenged by dynamic ocean environments and long offshore operations. These conditions place high demands on maritime situational awareness systems, which must ensure robust object detection and tracking while remaining cost-effective. This paper presents a multi-object tracking system specifically designed for autonomous ships, grounded in a deep understanding of their distinctive operational characteristics. The proposed architecture integrates multiple detection and navigation sensors with an AI-based perception algorithm and a probabilistic data fusion framework. With modularity and scalability at its core, the system processes sensor data through two specialized stages to ensure optimal performance. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through real-world trials under realistic maritime conditions. Beyond system performance, this study highlights the limitations of relying solely on local awareness systems in commercial maritime operations. It underscores the necessity for a standardized, systematic approach to generating and sharing positional data among vessels—via Next-Generation AIS and inter-ship communication. Drawing inspiration from structured environments in robotics, we suggest that such an approach offers a practical path to balancing operational safety with economic viability. Ultimately, this strategy may accelerate the adoption of autonomous vessels amid the complexities of modern maritime practice.

title: Collecting and Scheduling Demonstrations for Multi-Step Precision Manipulation with VLAs
abstract: We present a complete pipeline for applying vision-language-action (VLA) models to multi-step precision manipulation: an affordable, leader-free teleoperation system for collecting high-quality demonstrations, and a systematic study of how those demonstrations should be scheduled during fine-tuning. A single operator controls both arms and the mobile base of a Mobile ALOHA platform from one wireless gamepad, and uses this system to collect 608 real-robot episodes for a tube pickup-and-insertion task. Fine-tuning PI-0.5 with nine recipes that vary the placement and quantity of failure-recovery (correction) demonstrations shows that placement is the dominant factor: the same 51 correction episodes yield full-task success from 0.00 to 0.70 depending only on where they enter the schedule, and the winning three-stage recipe is also the fastest.

title: The COMPARE Ecosystem: Establishing Standards and Guidelines Towards Improving Open-Source and Benchmarking for Robot Manipulation
abstract: When developing a novel component of a robot system, researchers typically integrate open-source code for the remaining components in the pipeline, such as perception, grasp planning, and motion planning. However, there are several bottlenecks related to the accessibility and reproducibility of open-source which are stifling research, development, evaluation, and deployment of robots. To this end, we are working to develop community-driven guidelines for modular components in robot software pipelines in the context of picking in clutter. The architecture and methodology used to reproduce and integrate various open-source components into pipelines are reviewed, highlighting issues encountered along the way, and recommendations for improving accessibility and reproducibility using modular components are presented.

title: Clutter Metrics and Software Tools to Evaluate Multi-Object Scenes for Benchmarking Robotic Grasping and Manipulation
abstract: Dense cluttered scenes are a standard benchmark for evaluating robotic grasping algorithms, as they challenge grasp feasibility. Despite its widespread use, clutter is typically described qualitatively and lacks a consistent quantitative definition. Inconsistent scene descriptions can cause confusion in benchmarking and experiment set up, leading to incomparable performance results. To rectify this, we define clutter metrics as an initial step towards better benchmarking for robot manipulation, to improve performance evaluation across datasets, scenes, and algorithms. Using multi-view instance segmentation masks, we define two metrics: occlusion (where the visibility of objects is evaluated) and proximity (evaluating inter-object distance). The combination of these metrics allow clutter in multi-object scenes to be evaluated, providing a foundation for benchmarking of grasping across varying levels of clutter.

title: Size Estimation of Grasped Objects during Pick-and-Place using a Soft Finger with an Embedded IPMC Sensor
abstract: In this paper, we proposed a method for estimating the size of a grasped object during pick-and-place operations using a soft finger with an embedded IPMC sensor, implemented the system, and evaluated the estimation accuracy of the proposed method. As a result of experiments using cylinders with diameters of 60 mm and 70 mm, the diameter could be estimated in real time with an error of less than 0.1 mm even during pick-and-place operations.

title: SPIN-SLAM: Towards Real-Time Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM in Dynamic Environments
abstract: Autonomous agents need a precise mapping of dynamic environments containing humans, animals, or even objects they interact with to navigate efficiently and safely in the world around them. However, most SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) methods assume a static world, meaning they bake visual artifacts into the 3D map that hinders tracking and hurts visual fidelity. We demonstrate that the masking can be done 61.9x cheaper than the state-of-the-art while being within 0.6 dB PSNR of its rendering quality. Methods like WildGS-SLAM use the deep-feature model DINOv2 every frame and feed the output to an uncertainty MLP trained online. DROID-W drops the online mapping and uses the features more efficiently and reaches 13.03 FPS, but it still needs a depth estimator on every keyframe. However, the tracker used in these methods holds information that could be reused to mask the distractors: a temporal residual from its own pose/depth and a render of the live Gaussian map. Therefore, we do not need a semantic network and only retain a metric depth estimator queried every 10 keyframes only (20.6 ms amortized). We combine the Tracker and the Mapper more efficiently with an adapted shared memory and reduce the keyframe count without hurting quality with DiSC-KF, a Disambiguality-Scored Covisibility keyframe selector. We also apply two geometrical vetoes to remove static elements from the rough masks. We achieve 80.5 ms masking (101.1 ms with the amortized depth query) at 23.05 FPS, or 0.77x the sensor rate.

title: Resolving omnidirectional robot mobility with geometrical adaptability and structural rigidity via origami mecanum wheels
abstract: Exploration of unstructured, extreme environments requires miniature robots that can traverse heterogeneous terrains adaptively while maintaining sufficient structural rigidity for force-intensive tasks. However, conventional approaches often struggle to balance these requirements; they either lack the geometrical adaptability to handle irregular surfaces without compromising mobility or require bulky, complex mechanisms, which limits their use in confined spaces. This work resolves the conflict between miniaturization, mobility, adaptability, and rigidity through a Dual-Origami Mecanum Wheel Robot. This miniaturized platform integrates omnidirectional mobility with an inherently compliant yet load-bearing structure. By engineering deterministic motions for passive obstacle enveloping directly into the origami architecture, the robot surmounts irregular surfaces without active control. Crucially, the wheel actively expands its diameter from 50 mm to 70.8 mm, achieving the structural rigidity necessary to enable stable anchoring within narrow gaps. This capability allows the robot to neutralize high reaction forces, overcoming a fundamental limitation where small-scale robots typically lack the functional steadiness for high-load operations. Experimental results confirm that the platform surmounts obstacles up to 10% of its size without active reconfiguration. Furthermore, each wheel supports a payload 29.6 times its weight and successfully negotiates complex transition paths and diverse gap geometries. We demonstrate the platform’s multifaceted performance through practical exploration tasks, including debris removal and internal sample inspection via drilling. This synergy between adaptive locomotion and secure anchoring establishes a new design paradigm for multifunctional miniature robots capable of in-situ operational tasks in unstructured, extreme environments.

title: Deep Koopman Observer-based Robust Model Predictive Control against Learned-model Mismatch and External Disturbances
abstract: This study presents a deep Koopman observer based model predictive control (MPC) framework for accurate trajectory tracking in robotic manipulators, addressing the learned-model mismatch between the finite-dimensional Koopman predictor and the actual robot dynamics. To estimate the mismatch and external disturbances, deep Koopman observer is proposed, and the estimates are incorporated into the finite horizon prediction of the MPC. To guarantee the tracking-error stability of the proposed MPC, a finite-step relaxed control Lyapunov function constraint is proposed. Real-robot experiments under various fixed payloads demonstrate a reduction in root mean square error of up to 98.0% over conventional Koopman based MPC frameworks.

title: Expanding Assistive Robot Capabilities Through Inference, Feedback, and Control from Speech
abstract: Millions of individuals in the United States depend on in-home care to support their activities of daily living (ADLs), a demand that continues to rise alongside as a greater proportion of the population deals with age-related changes and chronic health conditions. Voice interaction is well-suited to this challenge because it offers users the ability to complete tasks in a ``hands-busy, eyes-busy'' manner and provides a low-effort means of control that supports accessibility, especially when user input is needed to ensure a task is done in a way that is safe and appropriate to their living context. We present a voice-first, multimodal interface for household assistive robots, the Inference, Feedback and Control from Speech (IFCS). ICFS is designed to support seamless and safe user-guided interactions within the physical domain. It combines an inference-enabled voice interface with a companion app for explicit user control and action transparency. IFCS is built on the foundation of a structured human-robot interaction consisting of multiple layers of input from the user prior to task execution. By utilizing an ordered process for task confirmation and adjustment, the IFCS system aims to improve reliability while remaining accessible to users with varying speech patterns and technological familiarity. Additionally, such an approach allows users to make quick changes to action plans if and when environmental information changes. For example, in a scenario where the user initially requests the robot to bring them a coffee but realizes that there is a more time-sensitive task that needs handling prior to confirming, like picking up groceries from the door, the user is able to clarify that the groceries must be picked up first then the coffee. In another case, if the robot is already delivering the coffee for the user, they are able to request the groceries task and utilize the companion app to blend the two task plans together. Future work should both evaluate the system as a whole and test the robustness of each of the three modules in diverse human-robot collaboration environments. Future work should conduct iterative user testing to explore how population variables, context, and individuals might influence the effectiveness of inference, feedback, and control. Beyond this, studies should consider how users see IFCS fitting into their everyday lives and workflows to evaluate real-world applicability and improve interaction design. A critical direction for future work is the integration of lightweight, local language models that can perform offline operations while maintaining sufficient inference capabilities. Finally, IFCS requires the collection of semantic environmental knowledge. In its current implementation, such data must be manually specified in a predefined structured format. For broader deployment, this process must be automated to allow the robot to independently perceive a semantic representation of its environment.

title: Dataset Development and Preliminary Study for Semantic 3D Skeleton Extraction in Precision Agricultural Robotics
abstract: A seasonal real tree dataset was constructed in a pear orchard environment using RGB-D cameras and LiDAR sensors under leaf-off conditions. The acquired 3D data provides detailed representations of trunk and branch structures in realistic orchard environments. RGB-D and LiDAR point clouds are integrated to generate dense tree representations, followed by ground removal and DBSCAN clustering for individual tree segmentation. ADTree-based modeling is then applied to each segmented tree to generate corresponding skeleton ground truths. The constructed ground truth represents the hierarchical branch topology of each tree and provides a basis for evaluating tree skeleton reconstruction methods. Additional data collection under leaf-on conditions is planned to investigate structural variations caused by foliage changes and enable seasonal comparison. The proposed dataset will be utilized for training and evaluation of a Flow Matching-based generative framework for tree skeletonization, supporting the analysis of skeleton reconstruction performance under realistic orchard conditions.

title: Multi-Contact Robot Dynamics with Saltation Matrices
abstract: When common hybrid dynamics simulations are applied to multi-legged locomotion and multi-fingered manipulation near multi-contact events, the number of mode schedules explodes combinatorially: contact can be made and in any of a factorial number of orders. We extend and confirm a prior theoretical prediction about a common class of these systems: when forces are additive and are switched based on position coordinates alone, the state-space flow is C1 (continuously differentiable). We experimentally verified this using a three-legged hopping robot. The three legs exert measurably different individual effects, but the combined triple collision is identical to first order across all 3!=6 mode schedules. This demonstrates that many systems long regarded as intractable because of the combinatorial explosion of mode schedules can be modeled and controlled through by linearization -- as if no multi-contact issue existed, and they were a C1 system.

title: ReturnNav: Bidirectional Topological Navigation from a Single Forward Demonstration
abstract: Abstract— Learned topological navigation models such as ViNT assume a unidirectional map: a single forward demonstra- tion is recorded, and the robot follows it once to a goal. Round- trip tasks—central to indoor delivery—require a second reverse demonstration, doubling operator effort. We present ReturnNav, a system enabling bidirectional navigation from a single forward demonstration with no retraining and no additional recording. ReturnNav applies three runtime mechanisms to an unmodified ViNT policy: (i) node-index reversal of the topomap, (ii) lateral image mirroring to compensate viewpoint inversion, and (iii) ViNT encoder re-localization at turnaround. Integrated with CARE monocular obstacle avoidance (∼48 ms on Jetson Orin), ReturnNav completes A→B→A round-trips with 5/5 arrival and zero collisions on a wide corridor, and generalizes to a symmetric narrow corridor (3/3 arrival) by replacing reactive APF with geometric depth-centering.

title: Toward Plug-and-Play Mapless AMR Navigation: A Hybrid Corrective Layer for Existing Navigation Controllers and Policies
abstract: Reliable autonomous mobile robot navigation in unknown real-world environments remains challenging in narrow passages and obstacle-rich settings. This extended abstract presents a controller-agnostic Hybrid Corrective Layer (HCL) that augments an existing navigation controller or policy without modifying or retraining the underlying system. The HCL comprises a Learned Corrective Controller (LCC), which generates obstacle-aware corrective commands from LiDAR-derived observations, and Proximity-Guided Action Arbitration (PGAA), which regulates the relative authority of nominal and corrective commands according to obstacle proximity. Real-robot experiments evaluate the HCL on two existing mapless navigation configurations: PID + Rule and Local MPC. In static-obstacle and narrow-corridor scenarios, adding the HCL improves robustness for both configurations. It enables successful narrow-corridor navigation where PID + Rule fails and improves Local MPC success while reducing proximity events and increasing obstacle clearance. These findings provide an evidence that HCL can serve as a collaborative, command-level augmentation for different existing controller designs, with potential extension to learned navigation policies through a compatible robot-command interface.

title: Latency Compensated Dynamic Object Grasping via Future Point Cloud Conditioning
abstract: Practical robotic systems often need to manipulate continuously moving objects, such as parts on conveyor belts, whereas many manipulation methods assume static environments. Under asynchronous control, the scene captured for inference can become outdated by the time the predicted action begins. Prior approaches address this mismatch using future robot states or image-based motion cues, but do not explicitly represent the target geometry at execution time. We estimate object velocity from recent observations and propagate the segmented object points over the delay interval to construct a latency-compensated future point cloud. The policy receives this representation together with the current observation. In moving-cube grasping experiments in Isaac Sim, our method outperforms both baselines, indicating the benefit of future 3D observations for latency compensation.

title: Stochastic Dynamics of Cyclic Decision-Making in Hierarchical Heteroclinic Networks
abstract: Stable Heteroclinic Channels (SHCs) provide an alternate dynamical systems framework for generating sequential activity patterns in biological and robotic control systems. For robotic applications, SHC-based decision networks must not only generate reliable sequences but also respond flexibly to sensory inputs that guide transitions between behavioral states. To generate complex robotics behaviors with this capability, we investigate a hierarchical SHC decision network that allows transitions among multiple behavioral hierarchies through externally applied biases that favor a desired hierarchy or decision state. However, residual activity from previous activations can influence future decisions in SHC networks, producing a memory-like effect that causes the system to repeat the same decision across cycles. This preference can exist after the sensory bias is removed, causing delayed transitions and reducing the ability of the network to return to unbiased decision-making. In this work, we study how stochastic perturbations affect memory and transition behavior in SHC decision networks during transient dynamics, defined here as the phase in which the system has been displaced from the heteroclinic channel and is evolving back toward it. These transient states are important for robotic control because sensory-driven switching, external noise, or changes in behavioral state may push the system away from the heteroclinic channel. Our results show that increasing noise amplitude attenuates the transient memory-like behavior, thereby improving the network’s responsiveness to the external perturbation during hierarchical switching. These findings suggest that appropriate selection of stochastic perturbations can improve behavioral flexibility by attenuating transient memory effects.

title: A Hybrid Haptic Simulator for Simultaneous Kinesthetic Feedback and Motion Rendering
abstract: The growing use of computer-aided design, virtual prototyping,and digital twins has increased the demand for evaluating physical human--product interaction before producing hardware prototypes. Although visual and auditory properties can be reproduced readily, physical interaction requires bidirectional exchange of force and motion. Conventional haptic interfaces primarily reproduce the force or torque perceived while a user manipulates a virtual object, whereas the resulting motion and stationary behavior of the physical interface are often treated separately or neglected. Reproducing both aspects is important for evaluating the perceived quality and functional performance of products during the design process. This paper presents a hybrid haptic simulator that simultaneously renders kinesthetic feedback and motion behavior. The interaction torque applied by an object to the user is interpreted as the combination of active and passive components. The active component stores, releases, or generates mechanical energy and can thereby drive motion. The passive component dissipates mechanical energy through effects such as friction and damping and always opposes motion. During motion, this direction-reversing passive component produces asymmetric interaction torque profiles for opposite movement directions. At rest, it acts as a reaction torque that adapts to and balances the applied external torque within the available passive resistance. Consequently, the interaction between the active and passive components determines both the torque perceived during manipulation and the resulting motion of the interface. To reproduce these distinct physical characteristics, the active component is rendered by an active actuator capable of injecting mechanical energy and initiating motion, while the passive component is rendered by a passive actuator that can only dissipate system energy. The proposed approach is validated by developing a hybrid haptic simulator for car door rendering. Experimental results and user evaluation show that the simulator reproduces both the asymmetric opening and closing torque profiles and characteristic motion behaviors of real car doors, including self-closing, holding, and settling.

title: Design and Preliminary Characterization of a Permanent Magnet Actuator for Attachment of Transhumeral Prosthetic Sockets
abstract: In conventional methods of attaching a prosthetic device to residual limbs, external forces from the external device must transduct through skin and soft tissue, before being borne onto internal bone. This process results in excessive stress and strain on the residuum of the user, which can in turn cause discomfort, pain, and injury. This type of mechanical connection is also suboptimal for manipulation, because positional and force (wrench) errors at the socket interface can propagate into precision error for fine manipulation tasks, when using a prosthetic device. One solution to this problem is osseointegration, in which mechanical abutments with the prosthetic device are attached directly to bone, through the skin. This approach circumnavigates the aforementioned problems with soft tissue, thereby alleviating discomfort and enabling better function across activities of daily living and a better quality of life. However, osseointegration carries with it a high risk of infection through the chronic wound around the abutment. In this work, we propose to use an actuated permanent magnet system to attach a prosthetic device to a ferromagnetic implant. This architecture maintains the impermeable skin envelop to protect against infection while alleviating stresses and strains on the soft tissue of the residuum. First, we illustrate design of a controllable axial-flux Halbach array (CAHA) that is suitable for transhumeral prostheses. Next, we show the mechatronic design that allows for actuation of this permanent magnet array. Finally, we show experimental results that characterize the prototype system, as-built, in quasistatic configurations with a mock ferromagnetic implant. These results set the stage for dynamic actuation in future work, wherein functional control algorithms will be implemented on the actuator to determine the utility of our proposed magnetic attachment method in transhumeral prosthesis attachment.

title: Evaluation of Strength Degradation of Synthetic Fiber Ropes Exposed to Short-Wavelength Ultraviolet for Lunar Applications
abstract: This study evaluates the strength degradation of synthetic fiber ropes for lunar applications under shortwavelength UV irradiation and repetitive bending. Tensile tests were conducted after UV exposure, repetitive bending, and their combined loading. The results show that Dyneema and Zylon exhibit significant UV-induced strength degradation, whereas Vectran and Kevlar maintain high strength efficiency. Under combined loading, the strength degradation was dominated by the factor causing greater degradation rather than by additive effects. These findings provide insight into the suitability of synthetic fiber ropes for cable-driven systems on the lunar surface.

title: Function-Based Structural Design of a 2-DOF Upper-Limb Exoskeleton for Active-Assistive Rehabilitation
abstract: Structural design of upper-limb rehabilitation exoskeletons has generally focused on achieving an adequate workspace, range of motion, and kinematic compatibility. In active-assistive rehabilitation, however, the assistive torque required from an exoskeleton varies according to the patient's residual muscle strength, indicating that structural design should also consider patient functional capability. Among structural design parameters, the center-of-mass (COM) location directly influences the required actuator torque and energy consumption during rehabilitation. This paper presents a structural design method for a two-degree-of-freedom (2-DOF) upper-limb exoskeleton intended for active-assistive rehabilitation. A human--exoskeleton coupled model was developed in the MATLAB/Simscape environment, where patient functional capability was represented using Manual Muscle Testing (MMT)-based active-assistive conditions. The required elbow actuator torque was then evaluated for different COM locations while maintaining identical rehabilitation motion and workspace. The analysis showed that the required actuator torque increased as the COM shifted toward the distal direction, and recommended COM ranges for the upper arm and forearm were identified. The proposed design criterion provides a quantitative guideline for considering actuator torque during the early structural design stage of active-assistive upper-limb exoskeletons.

title: Automated Robot Gas Sealing System for Prevention Gas Leakage on Coke Oven Door in Steelmaking
abstract: Gas leakage from coke oven doors is a persistent problem in coke production, causing environmental pollution, visibility issues, and serious safety risks for workers. Conventional sealing operations are performed manually by operators using semi-solid sealing material, exposing them to high-temperature, high-pressure, dust-filled, and hazardous environments. This paper presents an automated gas sealing system for coke oven door leakage prevention using a robot arm, a dedicated service car, and a vision-based localization strategy. The proposed system detects gas leakage locations at the control room, transports the robot to the target coke oven door via a service car, recognizes the leaking section using seam tracking and finding vision, and applies sealing material through an end-of-arm tool (EOAT). The system also supports remote monitoring and control, enabling safe and unmanned operation. The proposed automation framework is designed to eliminate direct worker exposure while improving sealing consistency and operational safety in coke oven environments.

title: Learning-Free Door-Opening Direction Estimation for Autonomous Wheelchairs Using a Single 360-Degree Camera
abstract: Autonomous wheelchairs have been deployed in airports, hospitals, and similar environments; however, their mobility is still limited because they cannot open or pass through standard doors other than automated ones. To navigate standard doors autonomously, a wheelchair must detect the door area, the door handle position, and the door-opening direction (left or right). Conventional approaches use onboard camera images and deep learning–based object detection to classify these elements into three classes: right-opening doors, left-opening doors, and door handles. However, this multi-class detection increases computational cost and is further constrained by the limited field of view of standard RGB cameras. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel method that equips a wheelchair with an omnidirectional camera. Using 360-degree images processed by YOLO11, the proposed method detects the door area and handle position, while the door-opening direction is determined without deep learning, based on the spatial relationship between the door and its handle. Experimental results show that, compared to the conventional method, the proposed approach improves performance, achieving a 2.5% increase in mAP50, a 5.4% increase in accuracy, and approximately a 5% improvement in F1- score across all detection classes. In addition, it achieves over 95% detection accuracy for objects within 4 meters and extends the detection range by 1 meter. These results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the conventional approach and is suitable for practical applications.

title: Development of an Earthworm-Type Robot Using a Side-Beam Bending Actuator for Large-Diameter Pipe Inspection
abstract: This study developed a lightweight, high-output earthworm-type robot using Side-Beam Bending Actuators (SBAs) to inspect large-diameter pipes in confined spaces, such as above ceilings. Reducing robot weight facilitates transportation, installation, and retrieval in elevated and confined spaces and reduces the load on pipes with limited structural support. At 0.20 MPa, each SBA generated pressing and contraction forces of 64 N and 440 N, respectively. A gripping unit comprising three SBAs generated 92 N, equivalent to 5.4 times the robot weight. The developed robot was 675 mm long and weighed 1.73 kg. Horizontal and vertical locomotion and passage through a 90° elbow were confirmed in a 250A pipe with an inner diameter of 254 mm. These results indicate its potential for inspecting curved, large-diameter pipes while reducing handling effort and pipe loading.

title: Experimental investigation of a planar three-link swimmer in viscous fluid
abstract: Locomotion of micrometer-sized swimmers in low Reynolds number environments is governed by viscous drag, demanding non-reciprocal periodic shape changes for propulsion. While Purcell’s planar three-link swimmer serves as a canonical theoretical model, analyzing its motion was significantly advanced by the geometric mechanics framework. However, validating these mathematically derived optimal gaits experimentally remains challenging due to unmodeled real-world fluidic and mechanical complexities. To demonstrate the results of the analysis, we developed an improved design of an untethered, macro-scale robotic surrogate. Operating in highly viscous silicone fluid to emulate the Stokes regime, this platform allows us precise control over the time-dependent shape variables. To reconcile our real robot’s physics—specifically the large added drag from its central flotation unit—we utilize a modified theoretical formulation that incorporates a central spherical drag element and calibrated drag coefficients for the non-slender links. Experiments were conducted using various ellipse-shaped gaits, generated by varying sinusoidal phase and amplitude shifts. By tracking the robot's motion with markers, the net displacement per cycle was determined as a function of the ellipse parameters. These experiments yielded counter-intuitive results, demonstrating a non-monotonic dependence of the net displacement as a function of phase and amplitude, as well as complete reversals in the swimming direction. These foundational experiments were utilized to extract and calibrate the parameters for the modified Purcell model. Following this, a physical demonstration was presented for bounded, large-amplitude gaits generated via optimal control and geometric analysis via height maps. Experimental validation confirmed that when bounding the physical joints angles, a non-smooth bowtie-shaped gait maximizes net forward displacement. This optimal bowtie-shaped gait outperformed the best ellipse-shaped gait by 5% and yielded more than double the displacement of the best circular gait. In conclusion, the experimental results demonstrated the motion of a 3-link Purcell-like robotics swimmer in a viscous fluid, proving the crucial role of combining theoretical model fitting, optimal control methods, and geometric analysis to determine the optimal gait.

title: Shoulder Torque Estimation for Exoskeleton Assistance using Upper-arm Forcemyography
abstract: This study proposes and compares two real-time shoulder torque estimation methods for a wearable shoulder exoskeleton, both driven by pressure-based sensing of the upper arm. Two silicone-covered barometric force sensors over the biceps and triceps brachii capture the antagonistic changes in muscle deformation and stiffness, and their signals are fused with a shoulder-joint encoder measurements. The indirect method estimates the elbow angle and the external load, and then computes the shoulder torque through a gravitational shoulder torque model, whereas the direct method maps the same features onto the torque. For three payloads not used during training, the indirect method achieved a torque RMSE of 3.19 Nm (R² = 0.62) and the direct method 1.42 Nm (R² = 0.87), indicating the benefit of removing sequential error propagation.

title: Procedurally generated high-fidelity 3D synthetic dataset for indoor building defect inspection
abstract: Indoor building defect inspection remains constrained by the lack of large, high-quality labeled datasets tailored to apartment interiors. During pre-occupancy inspection, defects must be identified reliably to support quality control and reduce rectification costs, yet manual inspection is time-consuming, subjective, and difficult to scale. Although deep learning has shown strong potential for automated defect detection, its practical deployment is limited by the scarcity of suitable training data. Existing public datasets are often focused on outdoor infrastructure, provide only low-resolution or classification-level labels, or lack the 3D spatial consistency needed for multi-view perception and embodied inspection systems. To address this gap, this project presents SynDefect3D, an open-source procedural framework for generating high-fidelity synthetic indoor defect data in navigable apartment environments. SynDefect3D is built on a 3D-native generation pipeline that procedurally synthesizes five common interior defect categories: crack, paint peel, spalling, paint bubble, and exposed wiring. Rather than modifying room-scale wall meshes directly, defects are generated as modular wall-attached assets, enabling fine morphological control while maintaining computational tractability. These defect instances are placed on apartment walls through constraint-guided rules that enforce realistic attachment and spacing conditions. The resulting scenes are assembled in sparse pre-occupancy apartment layouts and rendered with high-fidelity lighting, textures, and domain randomization to produce paired RGB images and pixel-accurate segmentation masks. The framework is fully seed-controlled, allowing for reproducible generation. Using this pipeline, the project releases a synthetic dataset of 27,680 annotated images at 1024 x 1024 resolution across 250 apartment room models. Each scene includes both room-level and defect-focused camera views, and five domain-randomization passes are applied to improve appearance diversity. The resulting dataset supports both semantic segmentation and object detection tasks. To validate dataset quality and usability, the project benchmarks multiple U-Net and YOLO models on the synthetic test split. Beyond synthetic benchmarks, the project also evaluates sim-to-real transfer. Models trained only on SynDefect3D demonstrate qualitative generalization to real apartment photographs despite domain shift. More importantly, when synthetic data is combined with a small manually annotated real dataset of 209 images, real-world object detection performance improves substantially, with mAP50:95 increasing by 359% relative to training on real data alone. Overall, SynDefect3D provides a scalable and reproducible foundation for training and benchmarking defect perception models, while also opening opportunities for future work in hybrid synthetic-real learning, embodied inspection, and robot-assisted building quality assessment.

title: When Search Becomes Memory: Accelerating Robot Design Discovery with Self-Evolving Skills
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as proposal generators for evolutionary robot design, yet most loops remain memoryless: simulator results shape the next population but are not preserved as reusable design knowledge. We present Auto-Robotist, a self-evolving LLM agent that distills morphology-search traces into an explicit natural-language skill library. Each skill stores a structural archetype, evidence-grounded positive and negative rules, and the evaluated designs that support them, making design memory inspectable rather than implicit in a population. During search, the agent retrieves skills to condition LLM edits of elite bodies while retaining a Genetic Algorithm (GA) mutation path for exploration; after evaluation, it updates the library through Add, Diagnose, and Merge. Across seven EvoGym tasks spanning locomotion, traversal, and object interaction, Auto-Robotist improves cold-start search and transfers learned skills to higher design spaces, where reference-conditioned transfer outperforms GA on every task. These results suggest that LLM agents can convert expensive physical evaluations into reusable, auditable design principles.

title: A Deterministic Ground Texture SLAM Simulator with Learned Ground Texture Fields
abstract: Ground texture localization and SLAM lack simulators that combine realistic imagery with a spatially consistent, revisitable world and controllable camera and trajectory conditions. We present a deterministic learned ground texture field that supports arbitrary physical-coordinate queries and renders user-specified trajectories and camera configurations with exact ground truth. We validate fields trained on four datasets and multiple hardware setups using texture comparisons, spatial-consistency tests, and matched real and simulated localization experiments. A real-photo mosaic reproduces most of the measured real–simulation gap, while tested camera and image effects do not, suggesting that observation-dependent appearance is a major challenge for ground texture localization. We then isolate camera-roll calibration error while holding the ground texture and robot trajectory fixed and find that small errors degrade visual odometry before GTBoW place recognition. Loop-closure correction improves trajectory error by $12.3times$ at $0.5^circ$ but provides no measurable benefit at $5^circ$, highlighting the importance of accurate camera extrinsic calibration for ground texture SLAM.

title: Graph-Based Context-Aware Robot Assistance Decision-Making for Human-Robot Collaboration
abstract: In human–robot collaborative assembly, robot assistance should be selected by considering the worker’s action, intention, tool use, part state, and task progress. However, conventional rule-based or finite-state-machine (FSM)-based assistance methods depend strongly on predefined task sequences, which can cause unnecessary or inappropriate interventions when the assembly order changes or recognition results are temporarily uncertain. This paper proposes a graph-based context-aware robot assistance decision-making framework for human–robot collaborative assembly. The proposed method uses recognized action, intention, tool, and part states to generate assistance candidates by combining an Intent Transition Graph and an Assist Policy Graph. It then applies ontology-based filtering, score-based selection, and intervention control using gating and cooldown conditions to select robot assistance actions that are consistent with the current assembly context. Preliminary validation in a chair assembly scenario shows that the selected assistance actions for nine assistance-required intent conditions were successfully completed in the execution layer. The average required assistance selection accuracy was 94.35%, and no unexpected robot assistance was observed in non-assistance intent segments. These results indicate that the proposed framework can select context-consistent robot assistance actions under flexible assembly sequences.

These results demonstrate that the developed robot combines lightweight construction and ease of handling with locomotion in large-diameter and complex pipe networks that are difficult for humans to access, indicating its potential to expand the applicability of in-pipe inspection.

title: Deep Learning-Based Framework for Efficient Multigoal Shortest Path Planning in Indoor Environments
abstract: Connecting multiple destinations with the shortest overall path in an obstacle-rich indoor environment is a classic problem in robotic path planning. Established solutions, such as A*, ARA*, and RRT*, execute faster when given smaller input maps that exclude extraneous paths. However, removing such paths without losing the ground truth solution is challenging, because runtime-efficient approximations can yield detours. This work proposes a deep learning-based Search-Space Reduction Pipeline (SRP) that integrates a module called MazeNet to solve indoor navigation tasks with fast runtimes while maintaining accuracy. We transform the indoor environment into a graph representation, reducing the planning task into a graph-based optimization problem known as the Obstacle-Avoiding Rectilinear Steiner Minimum Tree (OARSMT). MazeNet takes compressed images derived from graph abstractions as inputs and uses a recurrent convolutional neural network (RCNN) trained to predict the shortest feasible path connecting all destinations. Within SRP, MazeNet’s output restricts the search space for classical planners. MazeNet solves more complex instances than those seen during training via recurrence with an integrated termination condition. We evaluate MazeNet's runtime and path-length performance using a variety of planning methods against both exact and approximate graph algorithms in simulations and, after fine-tuning, in real-life floor plans. MazeNet solves all these specific test cases with improved runtimes and no increase in path length. Physics simulation further supports MazeNet's feasibility in the tested floor plans, with no recorded collisions during the navigation tasks.

title: Classical HSV vs. Fine-Tuned YOLO11n for Stop-Sign Detection on F1TENTH/RoboRacer
abstract: We deploy two stop-sign detectors on an F1TENTH/RoboRacer autonomous racing vehicle (NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, Intel RealSense D435i): a classical HSV-based pipeline and a fine-tuned YOLO11n model. We compare both across seven standardized track scenarios covering baseline detection, distractor resistance, multi-sign sequencing, and partial occlusion. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first direct on-car comparison of classical and deep learning sign detectors on the F1TENTH/RoboRacer platform. We also contribute a reusable evaluation protocol designed to stress each failure mode independently. YOLO11n eliminates all three false positives produced by HSV (3 FP -> 0 FP) while matching HSV on every scenario where HSV succeeds. Specificity measures how well a detector ignores non-stop signs; YOLO11n achieves perfect specificity (1.00) versus HSV's 0.63, meaning HSV triggers unwanted stops on distractors such as YIELD and ROADWORK signs that share red coloring or similar geometry. Sensitivity measures how reliably a detector catches true stop signs; across 11 stop signs, YOLO11n correctly detects 9 (sensitivity 0.82) versus HSV's 8 (sensitivity 0.73), with both false negatives tracing to detector-agnostic limits: one cooldown lockout and one 2/3-occlusion failure shared by both, and one additional cooldown FN unique to HSV in S2. A 5.5 MB YOLO11n model at one-fifth frame rate on the Orin Nano therefore achieves higher specificity and higher sensitivity than classical CV. This work is a precursor to an ongoing multi-class extension targeting 14+ sign categories, including traffic lights, on the same platform.

title: Wire-Guided Mobile Robot for Multimodal Inspection of Long-Distance Belt Conveyors in Steel Plants
abstract: Long-distance belt conveyors in steel plants are critical infrastructure for bulk material handling, yet their inspection remains challenging due to extended operating ranges, elevated installation, and harsh environmental conditions including dust, moisture, and falling debris, idler bearing degradation, roll misalignment, belt tearing, material accumulation, and overheating of drive components can lead to severe downtime and, in coal transport lines, fire hazards. Existing inspection practices based on manual patrols or fixed sensing systems are limited in scalability, localization accuracy, and cost-effectiveness over plant-scale conveyor networks. This paper presents a wire-guided mobile robotic system for autonomous multimodal inspection of belt conveyors in steel plants. The proposed platform travels along fixed steel wires installed beside the conveyor and integrates a detachable sensing suite consisting of an omnidirectional microphone. an RGB camera, and a near-infrared thermal imaging camera. While traversing the inspection route, the robot acquires synchronized acoustic, visual and thermal data for detecting abnormal idler behavior, belt surface damage, drive-unit overheating, smoke or fire symptoms, and excessive material spillage around guide rollers. Precise fault localization is achieved using encoder-based position tracking during robot motion. To enable reliable deployment in outdoor bulk-material environments, the system incorporates a mechanically stable wire-driven mobility structure, optional dual-wire support for enhanced safety under wind disturbance, and a docking station for wireless charging and standby operation. The collected multimodal data are segmented in temporal or frame-based units and processed by a deep-learning-based diagnostic framework that classifies conveyor conditions and issues graded alarms. To reduce plant-wide communication burden, only inference outputs and event-level information are transmitted to the control room. To proposed approach offers a practical alternative to dense installation of fixed monitoring devices by combining mobility, multimodal perception, and onboard intelligent diagnosis in a single inspection platform. It is expected to improve maintenance efficiency, enable early fault detection, reduce fire risk, and enhance the operational safety and reliability of long-distance conveyor systems in steel manufacturing environments.

title: Evacuation Planning for Multiple Drone Failures in Drone Light Shows
abstract: Drone light shows have emerged as a popular form of entertainment in recent years. However, several high-profile incidents involving large-scale drone failures---where multiple drones simultaneously fall from the sky---have raised safety and reliability concerns. To ensure robustness, we propose a drone evacuation algorithm specifically designed for multiple drone failures in drone light shows, aimed at mitigating the risk of cascading collisions by parking at safe locations during drone-dropping incidents. Our algorithm integrates a trajectory prediction to predict the trajectories of failing drones and employs anytime rapidly-exploring random trees algorithms to compute near-optimal evacuation paths that minimize the likelihood of surviving drones being hit by fallen drones. Our experiments showed that our approach can greatly increase the robustness of a multi-drone system by leveraging deep learning to predict the trajectories of fallen drones.

title: Cache-Age-Aware Reuse of VLM Representations for Efficient VLA Inference
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but they typically execute a large Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone for every action chunk, which introduces significant inference latency. We propose reusing the internal representation of the VLM across multiple action chunks, reducing the VLM execution frequency to once every K chunks. The Action Expert is explicitly conditioned on a reuse-stage embedding that indicates how outdated the cached VLM representation is, and a frozen lightweight vision transformer supplies up-to-date visual features for every action chunk through cross attention, compensating for short-term visual changes such as object displacement and robot motion. On the LIBERO benchmark, a single trained model allows the reuse period K to be varied at inference time: the success rate degrades gracefully from 97.0% (K=1) to 78.3% (K=5), whereas a baseline trained without the reuse-stage conditioning drops to 73.6% even at K=1 and below 58% for K>=2. The reuse reduces the mean per-chunk latency on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 from 498 ms (K=1) to 355 ms (K=3) and 322 ms (K=5), corresponding to speedups of 1.40x and 1.55x, so the reuse period can be selected according to the latency budget of the target platform without retraining.

title: A Soft Wearable Ankle Exercise Device with Event-Driven Phase Transition for Muscle Pump Activation
abstract: The muscle pump action, which prevents deep vein thrombosis (DVT), relies on the coordination between venous compression caused by triceps surae contraction and venous expansion caused by dorsiflexion. This study proposes an event-driven control scheme based on actuator tension and ankle angle for a soft wearable ankle exercise device driven by a high-stretch pneumatic actuator (HPA). Conventional fixed -duration control may reduce venous return by maintaining the resistive load longer than necessary. In a supine experiment involving ten healthy adult males, the proposed method achieved the highest blood flow velocity among all conditions. Compared with fixed-duration control, the proposed method resulted in lower triceps surae muscle activity and a larger range of motion (ROM), suggesting that phase switching based on the user's motion state enables both an appropriate resistive load and sufficient ROM.

title: Measuring the Question, Not the Answer: A Workshop Instrument for Probing Reflection on Machine Humanness
abstract: Humanoid robotics is organized around framing questions—whether a machine is humanlike, autonomous, or creative—but has no way to distinguish a question that produces reflection from one that produces a reflex. We propose treating such a question as an instrument and measuring its reflective yield: the degree to which engaging with the question changes a participant’s estimate of the question’s own importance. We report a pilot of a dual-probe workshop protocol, debuted at IACAP 2026, in which audiences answered both a direct question—Can a robot dance?—and a meta-question rating that question’s importance, before and after a structured debate. Across two surveys (n = 15 each), affirmative answers fell from 73.3% to 53.3% while rated importance rose from 3.40 to 3.80 on a five-point scale and the dismissive tail halved. Neither shift reaches significance at this sample size, and the surveys were unpaired; the contribution is therefore the instrument, its refinements list, and a powered design for the scaled study. We argue that dance is an excellent candidate for reflective yield because it forces a respondent up a layered taxonomy of humanness—morphological, kinematic, ecological, epistemic, ontological—in which each layer is harder than the one beneath it both to define and to realize, and because the verdict the question returns degrades monotonically the higher one climbs.

title: Anomaly Detection under Moving Viewpoints Using World Coordinate Features
abstract: Recently, labor shortage in retail stores is becoming severe, and the automation of product arrangement by robot is expected. Because there are countless states of products to be arranged, we defined them as anomaly products. We have developed a robot that detects them using an anomaly detection Neural Network (NN). However, conventional anomaly detection NNs are mainly designed for a fixed camera, making it difficult to detect multiple kinds of products over a wide area while moving. In this study, we focus on the world coordinates of products, which are independent of camera motion. We propose a novel anomaly detection NN using features extracted from an autoencoder that reconstructs the world coordinates. Experimental results showed that our method achieved a detection rate of 87.0 %, which was 12.6 points higher than a representative method for fixed cameras. In addition, a mobile robot equipped with our method successfully removed 85 % of anomaly products from a shelf.

title: Glance Globally, Restore Locally: Lightweight Tiled Dehazing of Native 4K Images for Robotic Vision
abstract: Unmanned robots must operate through sea fog and fire smoke, where camera-based perception degrades and onboard compute is limited. Native ultra-high-definition (UHD) dehazing must recover fine detail at 3840x2160, yet full-image processing with large networks is computation- and memory-heavy, while independent tile processing loses global haze, illumination, and color context. We present FLR-TileDehaze, a compact CNN-only method coupling a full-image low-resolution (FLR) guidance branch with overlapping high-resolution tile restoration, in two operating points: Lite (22.6K parameters) and Quality (33.6K; adds a global refinement and a low-resolution residual field). On a fixed local 1,562-image 4KID test split, Lite and Quality reach 17.76/17.88 dB PSNR, Quality improving all five evaluated metrics over Lite. On an RTX 3090, a frozen mixed-precision backend delivers 39-41 FPS native-4K model-path throughput without retraining, within 0.002 dB of FP32 validation PSNR. Among methods exceeding 30 FPS under this same-split protocol, our configurations achieve the highest PSNR, motivating resource-efficient preprocessing for high-resolution robotic vision.

title: MAROB-2500: A Severity-Stratified Blur Benchmark for Maritime Robot Perception with Object-Region Evaluation
abstract: Maritime robots face two blur sources at once: platform vibration blurs the whole frame, while target motion blurs the vessel far more strongly. Deblurring benchmarks model a single blur field and score with whole-image PSNR — blind to a vessel covering ∼1% of the pixels. We present MAROB-2500: 2,500 full-HD maritime electro-optical pairs with instance masks and per-image blur parameters. Blur is two-population (a background point-spread function plus a stronger vessel one, composited through a feathered mask), the excess given by ∆ = σ2 sh −σ2 bg — additive, and stable where the naive ratio is not. Evaluation is stratified over (σbg,∆), decorrelating both axes (|ρ| ≤ 0.05). Baselines leave the vessel 8.3–9.5 dB below the background; a change worth +0.76 dB overall is worth +1.74 dB on the vessel.
