title: nano-ros: Launch-Level Timing Contracts for ROS 2, Realized as Native RTOS Schedules
abstract: ROS 2 offers modular composition and a broad ecosystem, but no temporal semantics: a launch description specifies which nodes run, not the rates and deadlines they must meet. Production robots therefore pair a best-effort general-purpose computer as the main tier with a microcontroller-class safety island that closes actuation loops under millisecond deadlines and must remain safe while the main tier stalls or reboots. Embedded ROS 2 client libraries let a microcontroller join a ROS 2 system as a native node, but none declares timing at launch level; scheduling stays manual and platform-specific. This work presents nano-ros, a ROS 2 client library for RTOS and bare-metal microcontrollers, in which timing is a launch-level artifact: a platform-agnostic contract declares rates, end-to-end deadlines, chains, and criticality. The contract is checked statically; a priority-free ranking orders the workload, which is realized per kernel onto each RTOS's native scheduling mechanism, with any degradation recorded; the same contract compiles into static monitors enforced on target, and wire-protocol compatibility lets ROS 2 tooling interoperate unmodified.

title: Next Best View Selection for Object Pose Estimation based on Predicted Images at Next Views
abstract: Automating product display in retail stores requires accurate object pose estimation. Object pose is generally estimated using RGB-D cameras. However, simple-shaped products often lack sufficient visual information for accurate pose estimation from a single viewpoint. Therefore, active vision approaches improve pose estimation accuracy by moving the camera based on Next-Best-View (NBV) selection. However, conventional state-of-the-art methods rely on human-defined hypotheses that do not necessarily suit the characteristics of pose estimation neural networks. In this paper, we propose a novel NBV selection method based on a new metric called “pseudo-confidence.” Our method selects the next viewpoint based on the output of the pose estimation neural network itself. Before moving the camera, our method predicts the images that could be captured from candidate next viewpoints. By inputting these predicted images into the pose estimation neural network, we compute the pseudo-confidence for each candidate viewpoint. The next viewpoint is selected by maximizing this pseudo-confidence. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms conventional methods, improving the average pose estimation accuracy by 2.7 points. Furthermore, a robot equipped with our method successfully displayed 84.2% of products, achieving a 14.0-point improvement over the previous state-of-the-art method.

title: Intelligent Wheelchair Navigation Along Braille Blocks via Omnidirectional Vision and External Joystick Actuation
abstract: In countries such as Japan, where the population is rapidly aging, the burden on caregivers and nurses in nursing homes and hospitals is increasing. One of their main burdens is to assist in moving the patient/caregiver. Many of them are wheelchair users, and accompanying them to their destinations is burdensome. Electric wheelchairs have been developed as a way to reduce the burden, but they require the passenger to operate the wheelchair himself/herself, which places a burden on the wheelchair user. To solve these problems, we propose an all-sky camera mounted on an electric wheelchair to automatically detect Braille blocks in all directions by machine learning, and propose a traveling assistance system that automatically runs the electric wheelchair along the detected Braille blocks. First, Braille blocks are detected using You Only Look Once version5 (YOLOv5) on images obtained from a 360-degree camera. Then, the system determines the direction of travel based on the Braille block detection results. Next, the distance between the wheelchair and the Braille block is estimated. For the distance estimation, we propose a new method based on the equidistant projection method used to generate a 360-degree camera image. Based on this information, the joystick is operated to keep the wheelchair at a certain distance along the Braille blocks to assist the wheelchair in traveling. In this study, a new mechanism that can be installed in any type of electric wheelchair was developed to operate the joystick. In the verification experiment, the detection accuracy of Braille blocks in indoor and outdoor environments was 97.3%, the accuracy of determining the direction of travel was 100%, and the average error in measuring the distance between the wheelchair and Braille blocks was 0.15m. The proposed system was validated by the above algorithm, which enabled the wheelchair to run automatically.

title: Proposal of SkyWeaver : A Multi-Robot System for Assisting the Installation of Long-Span Metal Roof Panels
abstract: As the construction of large-scale buildings reaching up to approximately 200 m in width and 300 m in length continues to expand, roofing systems using long metal roof panels have become widely adopted. However, the conventional installation method requires extensive manual labor under harsh working conditions. This paper proposes SkyWeaver, a multi-robot construction-assist system that aims to automate the transfer, multi-point transport, and installation of long-span on-site-formed metal roof panels. SkyWeaver consists of three modules: Shuttle for transferring the panel onto rail trolleys, Convoy for cooperative multi-point supported transport, and Aligner for installation onto tight frames. Following a staged development strategy, we built prototypes of Shuttle and Convoy and experimentally examined feasibility. Shuttle supports the panel tip with a roller-based end-effector and synchronizes its motion by estimating the panel feed velocity from roller rotation. A 4 m tracking demonstration confirmed stable tip support while following the moving panel. For Convoy, we target panels up to 200 m with an 8 m rail pitch, which results in up to 25 support trolleys and a payload up to 1000 kg. A scaled transport test using five trolleys with a 27.6 m panel over an 8 m out-and-back run demonstrated multi-point support and operator-commanded convoy motion.

title: CVLAMP: Compliant Vision Language Action Movement Primitives
abstract: We present Compliant Vision-Language-Action Movement Primitives (CVLAMP), a closed-loop framework for contact-rich dual-arm manipulation. CVLAMP conditions a VLA backbone on images, language, Cartesian state, and force history, decoding a compact Cartesian motion primitive in place of a dense action chunk. Each primitive couples a Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) pose rollout with shared-phase wrench and gripper profiles, executed by a phase-governed controller that can run, slow, hold, or abort from real-time feedback. The architecture extends a pretrained π0.5 flow-matching VLA with cross-attention-fused state and force encoders, trained with a composite regression, rollout-consistency, and mode-classification objective via staged, single-GPU LoRA adaptation of the released checkpoint. In simulation, the model localizes the goal object from vision alone with a mean 2D position error of approximately 5.5 cm on held-out, previously unseen object positions, and the closed-loop system reliably approaches and grasps the target object; full task completion and real-robot deployment are ongoing work.

title: Toward Conversational VLMs: A Pilot Taxonomy of Robot Response Decisions from Wizard-of-Oz Assistive Interaction
abstract: Robots that follow natural-language instructions in everyday indoor environments must act on incomplete human utterances. Instructions often omit essential information, such as the identity of an out-of-view object, an intended destination, or the user's goal. Existing datasets contain little real-world situated dialogue and provide few practice-grounded criteria for deciding when a robot should act, confirm, clarify, or refuse. We retrospectively analyze a pilot Wizard-of-Oz study in which five participants performed everyday indoor tasks, including door opening, drawer opening, feeding, drinking, and cleaning, with a wheelchair-mounted mobile manipulator while the wizard responded without a prescribed asking policy. This preserved authentic user behavior but produced inconsistent robot-side decisions, motivating an explicit decision scheme. From 40 episodes, we derive a two-level taxonomy of six response modes (ANSWER, REPORT_DONE, REFUSE, CONFIRM, CLARIFY, ACT) and four ambiguity types (intent, referential, spatial, intelligibility). Two human annotators and an AI annotator applied the scheme to the pilot data. Clean-label rates were 91% and 89%, and Cohen's kappa ranged from 0.72 to 0.96 across decision-point, mode, and ambiguity levels for both human-human and human-AI comparisons. Fine-tuning LLaVA-1.6-7B on taxonomy-derived labels for ACT and CLARIFY indicates the feasibility of training vision language models using annotations from our taxonomy. Remaining boundary cases in decision-point identification and REPORT_DONE motivate a constrained protocol for standardized dialogue collection.

title: Where Must the Thermal Memory Live? Self-Sensing Displacement of a Shape-Memory-Alloy Coil Through the Unpowered Cooling Phase
abstract: Abstract—We estimate the displacement of a shape-memory- alloy (SMA) coil from only the voltage and current its constant- current driver already produces, and ask where the required thermal memory must live: in the network, or in the features? A fixed, untrained bank of four leaky integrals of electrical power (τ = {1, 2, 4, 8} s) feeds a small recurrent network: 119 ± 11 μm test RMSE (1.5 % of stroke) at 10 Hz on 264 cycles of a Flexinol coil, through the unpowered cooldown. A nine-variant phase- resolved ablation localizes the mechanism: the bank matters most exactly where the drive goes silent, and under extrapolation the model with no recurrence becomes the best one — dynamics fixed by physics transfer where fitted dynamics do not.

title: CR-VSCP: Evidence-Gated VLM Semantic Constraints for Autonomous Driving with Reduced HD Map Dependency
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide traffic semantics that are difficult to encode geometrically, but se- mantically plausible outputs may still be physically inconsis- tent. In this paper, we propose the Coarse-Route-guided VLM Semantic Constraint Planner (CR-VSCP), which treats VLM outputs as event hypotheses rather than motion commands. Candidate trajectories first pass VLM-independent feasibility checks for collision avoidance, drivable-area compliance, and vehicle-dynamics constraints. A VLM event can affect candidate ranking only after Evidence-Gated Verification (EVG) confirms route consistency and independent physical evidence. On 12,147 NAVSIM navtest frames, the complete planner achieves a PDM Score (PDMS) of 0.810. On held-out semantic-event data, EVG increases stop/yield precision from 15% to 47–57% and reduces false stops from 26% to 6%. A log-clustered bootstrap over 57 driving logs further shows that direct lateral VLM intervention significantly degrades planning performance. These results sup- port a division of responsibility in which VLMs interpret non- geometric driving semantics while an explicit planner retains authority over trajectory geometry and hard safety constraints.

title: Fine Wrist Control as a Marker of Surgical Teleoperation Expertise
abstract: Unlike most intensely physical pursuits, training for teleoperation of surgical robots focuses primarily on task outcomes rather than surgeon body posture or biomechanics during task completion. Toward the question of the role of biomechanics in surgical expertise, we sought to characterize the articular motion of expert teleoperators as compared to novice users. Twenty-seven novices and nine experts completed a non-medical cylinder-on-peg transfer task while their upper limb biomechanics were recorded via motion trackers. During more difficult motions, experts stabilized their wrist motion more than to novices, while maintaining adequate range of motion in their shoulder and elbow and completing the task significantly faster than novices. This marker of expertise suggests the importance of attention to user biomechanics during teleoperation of surgical robots.

title: A Control Strategy for Reproducing Gait-Related Ankle Motion in the Supine Position Using a Hyper-Extension Pneumatic Actuator

title: A Novel On-Gait Energy-Recycling Knee Exoskeleton Using an Active Regeneration Strategy
abstract: This study proposes an on-gait energy-recycling knee exoskeleton that integrates positive-work assistance, negative-work assistance, and energy regeneration. These results demonstrate energy-efficient exoskeleton operation by integrating assistance and energy regeneration within a single gait cycle, potentially extending the operating time of wearable robots.

title: Residual-Corrected Implicit Mechanics for Actionable Digital Twins of Cable-Driven Soft Robots
abstract: Accurate control of cable-driven soft robots is limited by the sim-to-real gap caused by hysteresis, fabrication variability, unmodeled external loads, and other model-form errors. We present a residual-corrected digital twin that combines discrete elastic rod (DER) simulation with data-driven correction and causal self-evolution. The DER model captures the robot’s deformation and provides physically grounded equilibrium sensitivities for gradient-based control. A compact multilayer perceptron learns the Cartesian residual between simulated and real robot's tip positions using normalized cable lengths, simulated tip coordinates, and payload information. The corrected model is embedded in a receding-horizon inverse-kinematics controller that propagates tracking errors through equilibrium constraints using adjoint sensitivities and generates bounded cable-length commands. To improve the deployed twin, we introduce a causal self-evolution loop that preferentially samples reachable targets in regions where the current model exhibits larger errors, plans motions in simulation, executes the resulting commands on the physical robot, records new motion-capture residuals, and retrains the model on the expanded dataset. Across 4,140 samples, the residual model reduces the mean 3D tip error from 18.58 mm to as low as 4.60 mm. When used for inverse-kinematics tasks, the corrected twin reduces the control error from 25.2 to 9.9 mm, while closed-loop refinement achieves a mean terminal error of 1.7 mm. These results demonstrate that physics-guided residual learning can transform an imperfect mechanics model into a data-efficient, self-evolving, and actionable digital twin for soft-robot control.

title: Perception-Aware Trajectory Planning for Robust LiDAR-Inertial Odometry on Quadrotors
abstract: LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) is increasingly suitable for uncrewed aerial vehicles as LiDAR sensors become smaller, lighter, and more affordable. We analyze how environmental geometry affects the information available to point-to-plane LIO using the Fisher information matrix (FIM). We then introduce a sampling-based trajectory planner that evaluates the predicted FIM along candidate trajectories to improve future LiDAR observation quality and estimation robustness. Hardware experiments across three paired flight conditions show that the planner accomplishes the specified mission while achieving a geometric-mean increase of 39% in the information determinant relative to the perception-agnostic baseline.

title: Kresling Origami Structure based Haptic Device for Gripping Feedback
abstract: Haptic feedback improves the accuracy and stability of teleoperated gripping, where both normal force and tangential torque at the fingertip govern grip control. Rendering such multimodal feedback within a compact, fingertip-scale device, however, remains challenging. We present a Kresling-origami-based haptic device that delivers simultaneous normal, torsional, and vibrotactile feedback from a single compact structure. Kresling dipole, composed of two mirror-symmetric Kresling cells, is driven by a central neodymium magnet and two coaxial coils. Since axial and rotational motions are coupled in the Kresling structure, the structure converts a purely linear electromagnetic force into normal and torsional feedback. The device delivers normal force up to 0.95 N and torque up to 4.53 N·mm with a response time of approximately 8 ms, and could also deliver vibrotactile feedback up to 250 Hz.

title: Human Control Strategies in Haptic Teleoperation Environments
abstract: Robotic teleoperation allows humans to remotely interact in environments, improving safety and accessibility in industries like medicine, manufacturing, and search and rescue. Haptic feedback provides additional information about the environment, which is particularly valuable when visual information is insufficient. For instance, when navigating with an occluded lens during robotic teleoperated surgery. Even with environmental forces reflected back to the operator through haptics, successful teleoperated movement can be difficult in scenarios with limited vision. Shared control between the human operator and robot can help reduce this burden. Yet, in order to share control effectively, a robot must first identify operator intent and control strategy. In this work, we uncover differences in human movement control strategies when exploring then completing a one-shot task in nonlinear, position-dependent force environments through a robotic manipulandum. We classify human movement into three possible strategies based on physically interpretable control models: (1) minimum jerk; (2) minimum effort, jerk-penalized; and (3) modulated power. Control strategy classification significantly predicted both peak velocity and peak proxy impedance values during the trials. This work is a first step towards classifying human strategies in nonlinear teleoperation environments so that robots can assist humans in using these strategies more effectively.

title: Query-gated Dual-View Fusion for Submillimeter-Precision CNC Lathe Manipulation
abstract: Loading a ring-shaped metal workpiece into a CNC lathe chuck requires submillimeter alignment: even a small visual error can cause the final insertion to fail. The robot must first establish the global spatial relationship between the workpiece and the chuck, and then resolve fine workpiece--chuck geometry near contact. A head camera provides the global spatial location of the workpiece, whereas a wrist camera resolves the fine alignment between the workpiece and the chuck; therefore, the relative importance of the two views varies across different stages of the task. We present a query-gated dual-view policy that preserves dense patch tokens from a frozen vision encoder, retrieves task-relevant evidence independently from each view, and adaptively fuses the retrieved features at the query and channel levels. The fused visual representations, together with proprioceptive history, condition a diffusion decoder that predicts future action chunks. Trained on 600 real-robot trajectories, the policy achieves 100% insertion success in the nominal setting (50/50 trials). It further succeeds in 71/100 trials under positional perturbations of up to 20 mm and in 67/100 trials under rotational perturbations of up to $4^circ$. These preliminary results suggest that explicitly routing complementary global and local visual evidence is a promising interface for precision visuomotor control.

title: A Canonical-View Dataset for Studying Sim-to-Sim and Real-to-Sim Visual Matching of Manipulator URDF Bundles
abstract: The Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) is a widely used standard format for defining robot structure and kinematics across simulators. This work builds a canonical-view rendering dataset of manipulator URDF bundles. Each manipulator URDF bundle are rendered from four fixed views, isometric, front, side, and top, in both MuJoCo and PyBullet. Using this dataset, two questions are studied. Q1 (Sim-to-Sim): how differently do different simulators render the same URDF bundle? To address this question, a cross-simulator visual similarity study is conducted. Q2 (Real-to-Sim): given an image of a real robot, can its corresponding URDF bundle be identified based on its appearance? To address this question, a preliminary visual-embedding-based pipeline is proposed.

title: Human-guided RL-based Cooperative Manipulation for Dual-arm Agricultural Robots
abstract: This study proposes a human-guided RL-based cooperative manipulation method for dual-arm agricultural robots performing various farming tasks in complex environments. By combining imitation learning and reinforcement learning, the proposed method enables the system to learn efficient and stable manipulation strategies while reducing reliance on manually designed control rules. First, the system learns human behaviors related to farming tasks through behavior cloning (BC), and then refines the learned policy using the proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm to enhance robustness and adaptability across diverse agricultural environments. This enables the system to mimic complex dual arm cooperative behaviors, such as performing a primary task with one arm while removing obstacles with the other, allowing efficient operation even in complex and irregular environments. Through this study, agricultural robots are expected to perform tasks in a human-like manner across complex and diverse agricultural environments.

title: Coarse-to-Continuous Projected Force-Manipulability Optimization for a Quadruped Manipulator
abstract: When a quadruped manipulator performs contact tasks such as pulling, it must not only reach a target end-effector pose but also select a whole-body posture that can efficiently transmit force along the desired interaction direction. This study proposes a coarse-to-continuous optimization method that optimizes a nine-dimensional arm–base state consisting of six arm joints, trunk backward offset, trunk height, and trunk pitch, given a target end-effector pose and pulling direction. First, 125 coarse seeds are generated, and candidates satisfying inverse-kinematics and support conditions are ranked according to directional force manipulability (DFM). Post-optimization including analytic projected-gradient refinement is then applied to the top-ranked candidates to increase DFM while preserving the target end-effector pose. Final candidates are selected according to their DFM ranking after evaluating collision, support feasibility, actuation limits, and path feasibility. The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated against a 125-seed grid-only method and an 891-seed dense grid-only method in terms of end-effector pose accuracy, DFM, and optimization time.

title: Whole-Body Representation for Point-Cloud-Conditioned Motion Distillation in Mobile Manipulation
abstract: This study investigates which robot representation is most effective for whole-body expert motion distillation in mobile manipulators. In particular, it examines whether Cartesian robot geometry aligned with the scene is sufficient, or whether explicit kinematic structure is also required. Five representations are compared by combining configuration coordinates (𝑸) with collision-sphere geometry ( 𝑪𝑺), kinematic keypoints (𝑲), and sampled robot mesh geometry (𝑴𝒆𝒔𝒉). All variants are trained on the same cuRobo expert trajectories and evaluated using held-out expert-action prediction and closed-loop execution. Q+K+CS achieves the best overall performance, reaching 75.3% goal success, 65.3% safe success, and 84.8% collision-free execution. These results indicate that spatial alignment alone is insufficient and that the effectiveness of Cartesian robot geometry depends on how collision-relevant occupancy and kinematic structure are represented.

title: Design Evolution of Insect-Scale Climbing Robots: Toward a Miniaturized Steerable Robot with Surface Transition Capability
abstract: Insect-scale climbing robots can access narrow and complex environments that are difficult to reach with conventional robotic platforms. However, miniaturization introduces severe limitations in the available space, payload, and actuation capability. At the same time, the small mass of such robots provides opportunities to employ simple and inexpensive attachment mechanisms. In our previous work, we demonstrated a 40-mm-long climbing robot using commercially available dry adhesives that achieved vertical, inverted, and surface-to-surface locomotion. More recently, advances in micro-scale 3D printing enabled the fabrication of miniature planetary gears, allowing further miniaturization and differential steering using micro-ultrasonic motors. Building on these developments, we developed a 30-mm-long, 10-mm-wide adhesive robot with independently driven front wheels for active steering. The robot successfully navigated obstacles on horizontal and vertical surfaces while performing a concave surface-to-surface transition. These results demonstrate the integration of climbing, steering, and surface transitions in a compact insect-scale platform.

title: Geo-Referenced Detection of Beaver Lodges from Oblique UAV Thermal Imagery
abstract: We are trying to turn hours of oblique thermal UAV video from Alaskan winter surveys into a short list of map coordinates that an ecologist can check on foot for beaver lodges. Beaver expansion into the Arctic can accelerate permafrost thaw by increasing surface water, so ecologists track where lodges appear, and ground surveys are slow across remote or frozen terrain. Direct geo-referencing would automate the search, but it maps a pixel to a world-frame ray and intersects it with terrain, so orientation error strongly affects long-range locations. Our own earlier pipeline assumed a near-nadir camera; the recorded orientation was 30 to 77 degrees off nadir, and the nadir projection under-ranged detections by 8.2, 21.9, and 12.1 times on three sampled segments. We replace that assumption with a pitch-, roll-, and yaw-aware ray intersection carrying a range uncertainty on every fix, and we redesign detection around gain-invariant local contrast with a per-row gate for 3 to 12 m structures, since automatic gain makes fixed grey thresholds unreliable. On 73,454 frames from three flights near Fairbanks, the corrected geometry reduced static-feature reprojection spread from 21.1 m to 1.4 m and from 10.4 m to 1.8 m, with a yaw-flipped control confirming the logged yaw convention. A domain expert reviewed 283 spatially sampled frames and marked nine lodges, and their spread similarly decreased from 21.5 m to 5.2 m. Match rate alone is uninformative here: the unfiltered pipeline returns 1,379 candidates, and 88% of arbitrary surveyed points lie within 10 m of one, so matching all nine lodges gives only 1.13 lift over chance. The projection geometry supplies a filter: a ground-lying structure is vertically compressed by approximately sin(depression) while an upright structure is not, and rejecting detections taller than 1.2 times this prediction removes 76% of candidates, retains all nine lodges, and raises lift to 2.18 (p = 0.001). The labels reflect expert recollection rather than field verification; nine lodges is too small to characterize a detector, and the shape threshold was selected on the labeled set. A second Alaskan campaign is collecting radiometric imagery with surveyed lodge coordinates, which removes the gain dependence and supports direct precision and recall measurement. We favor recall throughout, because an expert can reject false positives while a missed lodge never reaches review.

title: Vision-Language Robotic Instrument Handover for Operation
abstract: Instrument handover is one of the most repetitive and timing-sensitive tasks in an operating room, and it degrades with staff fatigue. We present a vision-language prototype that turns a spoken instrument request into a physical handover on a bench that mimics an operating room. Recognition runs a three-stage cascade: a local prototype classifier matches a whole utterance, SenseVoice-Small transcription is matched against an instrument lexicon and a per-surgeon alias table, and acoustic template matching acts as a fallback. A short enrollment mode adapts the recognizer to each surgeon in Mandarin, Cantonese, or English. An OpenPI vision-language-action model, fine-tuned on a surgical-instrument dataset, returns the target region for six instrument classes, and the arm replays a per-instrument trajectory. Emergency abort, exit, and a task cooldown sit outside every learned module. Across 360 end-to-end trials, the prototype completed 90.28% of handovers, with 4.719 s mean voice response and 14.688 s mean delivery.

title: One-Shot Grasp Adaptation for Tightly Packed Scenes via Prior-Guided Recovery of Affordance Regions
abstract: Robotic grasping in tightly packed scenes remains challenging due to the limited availability of grasp affordance regions. Existing vision-based recognition and grasp detection methods often struggle to generalize across domains and require scene-specific data for reliable adaptation, resulting in substantial annotation effort and computational cost. To address these limitations, we propose a one-shot adaptation framework for grasp detection in tightly packed scenes. The framework requires only a single RGB-D observation and autonomously generates training data without manual annotation. A prior-guided affordance recovery method is introduced to identify undetected or misdetected graspable regions, followed by primitive fitting for robust grasp planning and label generation. The generated labels are further augmented through simulated object translations, while an optimized loss function enables efficient fine-tuning of an existing grasp detection model. Real-world experiments demonstrate effective adaptation across varying object numbers, randomized arrangements, and novel instances in tightly packed scenarios.

title: Monocular Indoor Navigation with Visual–Floor-Plan Alignment and a Reactive RL Policy
abstract: We present an indoor navigation framework that combines visual–floor-plan alignment, implemented through cross-modal grounding, with a reactive reinforcement-learning (RL) policy. The only exteroceptive sensor is a monocular RGB camera; a human-oriented 2D floor plan provides the global spatial reference. The alignment module provides a grounded pose that yields the relative goal distance and bearing; the policy generates local motion from the current segmented image. We compare two configurations that share the same PPO policy and differ in the source of this relative goal. On fixed Route 1, in a simulated area excluded from training, Proposed completed 20/20 repeated trials and Odometry + PPO 13/20; a LiDAR-based AMCL + Nav2 reference also completed 20/20. Successful example trajectories were obtained on Routes 2 and 3 as qualitative evidence only. Grounded-pose trajectories show visible offsets near symmetric branches, which did not prevent the robot from reaching the goal.

title: Betting for Sim-to-Real Performance Testing
abstract: Roboticists are, in some sense, gamblers: every sim-to-real deployment is a wager that simulation-implied performance will carry over to real-world hardware. This paper formalizes that wager for sim-to-real performance testing (i.e., given a fixed policy, controller, or robotic system, whether model-based, learning-based, or hybrid, as it stands, one seeks to test its performance under a certain real-world environment for validation, regulation compliance, and other purposes). Specifically, we bring scaled simulators to facilitate real-world robot performance inference and certificate through the perspective of ``betting''. This allows practically efficient (i.e. with few real-world tests) and provably accurate (i.e. close to ground truth measure) performance tests of various robotic systems. Within the inference tasks, the sim-to-real bet induces a bet-weighted estimator that provably outperforms Monte Carlo and composes with importance sampling for rare events. Within the certificate tasks, the same bet accumulates an e-process, and the candidates it never rules out form an anytime-valid certificate, valid whether or not the bank of simulators is any good. Extended experiments are performed across a variety of applications including synthetic examples, robotic manipulation, locomotion, and navigation tasks.

title: Zero-Shot Transfer of a Map-Free Reinforcement Learning Navigation Policy from a Differential-Drive Robot to a Quadruped Robot
abstract: A map-free deep reinforcement learning (DRL) navigation policy, trained entirely in simulation for a differential-drive robot, is transferred zero-shot to a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot, with no additional training or fine-tuning on the new platform. Semantic segmentation bridges the visual gap between simulation and reality by generating binary visual observations consistent with those used during training, while self-localization is provided by a stereo visual-inertial odometry (VIO) pipeline that requires no prior map or LiDAR. Real-world experiments in an indoor corridor demonstrate stable, long-distance autonomous navigation, confirming that a navigation policy learned for a differential-drive robot transfers zero-shot to a quadruped platform.

title: Encoder-Free Hexapod Dead Reckoning on Sand Using Learned Inertial Correction
abstract: For inexpensive legged robots traversing remote natural terrain, minimal-sensing localization strongly affects autonomous range and search efficiency. Although proprioceptive sensors such as inertial measurement units (IMU) are compact and widely used on robotic platforms, direct integration of noisy inertial measurements causes small sensor errors to propagate into large pose estimation errors, limiting their use as independent dead reckoning sensors. In this work, we address drift in encoder-free dead reckoning by combining body-frame acceleration profiles from a compact multi-IMU array with commanded motion parameters in a convolutional neural network (CNN) bias estimator. The estimator predicts the difference between commanded and realized platform displacement, without using joint encoders or explicit terrain labels. In outdoor local search experiments with an encoder-free hexapod robot, the proposed approach reduces mean dead reckoning drift by approximately 41% on grass and 59% on sand relative to an idealized commanded-kinematics baseline. These results indicate that a platform-specific dataset collected in controlled indoor terrains improves outdoor dead reckoning performance, even when the deployment terrain is not fully represented in the training dataset. This method provides a low-cost, compact proprioceptive drift reduction method for minimally instrumented legged robots when exteroceptive localization is unavailable due to cost or environmental conditions. We expect this approach to be helpful in developing future low-cost robots for scrambling across extraterrestrial, underwater, or underground granular media where leg slip is both common and hard to predict.

title: Delivered Does Not Mean Usable: Communication-Service Limits in Distributed Robot Localization
abstract: Communication-efficient distributed localization is usually motivated by reducing the estimator payload exchanged between robots. We show that this view hides a second requirement: remote motion must first be served by the network and must still be temporally admissible when it reaches the estimator. We characterize a D-CLIPSE-based UWB realization with finite network-wide ranging and state-exchange service, transaction-local carriage of preintegrated relative motion increments (RMIs), and optional passive listening (PL). Separating source-service coverage $C^{S}$ from temporal usability $U^{T}$ yields effective real-motion coverage $C^{M}=C^{S}U^{T}$. Across 68 conditions and 680 trials, $C^{M}$ is strongly associated with held-state accuracy ($rho_S=-0.95$), whereas the nominal exchange rate is not. PL recovers missing service without additional transmissions, yet higher exchange activity reduces temporal usability and passive reception carries a substantial modeled RX cost. A registered sentinel shows that complete delivery can coexist with zero usable motion.

title: Weld-PICA: Traceable and Uncertainty-Aware Human-in-the-Loop Evidence for GMAW Weld Inspection
abstract: End-to-end AI systems increasingly combine perception and language models to turn sensor data into human-facing assessments. Their outputs, however, are difficult to review when confidence scores are detached from source evidence, generated descriptions contain unsupported details, or uncertainty from different modules is collapsed into one value. We present Weld-PICA, a human-in-the-loop framework that converts object detections into source-linked, crop-grounded evidence records with explicit uncertainty and bounded interaction. Gas metal arc welding (GMAW) defect inspection provides the current case study, but the design applies more broadly to detection-plus-vision-language workflows in which a person retains decision authority. The offline prototype links YOLOv7 detections, padded crops, local vision-language observations, and stable finding identifiers. We describe the interaction model and a planned evaluation spanning detection, evidence grounding, and ProbVLM-style semantic uncertainty.

title: Geometric Modeling and Hardware Validation of a Coaxial 3-RRR Manipulator for Spherical Inverted Pendulum Stabilization
abstract: This work presents the modeling, design, and experimental validation of a coaxial 3-RRR spherical parallel manipulator (SPM) for spherical inverted pendulum (SIP) stabilization. The pendulum configuration is represented by a point on the unit sphere, and the platform orientation by a rotation matrix in SO(3). By locating the pendulum pivot at a fixed offset from the SPM remote center, platform rotation generates translational pivot acceleration that directly actuates the pendulum dynamics. A physical prototype with closed-loop stepper actuation, encoder feedback, real-time inverse kinematics, and inertial orientation sensing was developed. Preliminary experiments demonstrate tracking of a 180-degree platform maneuver over 2 seconds with a maximum orientation error of 7.30 degrees, establishing a modeling and hardware basis for future closed-loop SIP stabilization.

title: Design, development and field tests of an ASV-AUV system for iceberg mapping.
abstract: Icebergs, originated from glacier discharge and ice sheet calving, are a significant freshwater source in the polar oceans. Over their lifespan, icebergs drift toward lower latitudes and release freshwater as they melt, which can affect local environments and potentially influence large-scale ocean processes such as sea-level rise and the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). To better quantify its climate impacts and iceberg drift models, more information about their shapes and the surrounding water properties has to be collected. Herein, we present the design, development and field validation of Robotic Iceberg Sentinels (RISE), a multi-robot system consisting of an Autonomous Surface Vehicle and an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle. The RISE system (hardware & software) enables multi-robot cooperation for mapping natural and man-made structures such as icebergs, glacier fronts and offshore wind-farms.

title: Swimming Like a Crab: Multi-modal Legs with Flippers for Hexapod Robot Swimming and Walking
abstract: Mobile robots are increasingly capable of exploring complex aquatic and transient environments. They must do so for a multitude of reasons such as underwater exploration, inspection, and repairs. Currently, remotely operated vehicles are capable of exploring ocean environments with propellers for locomotion, but are not designed to interact with complex regolith or traverse constrained rocky terrain. Furthermore, the lack of underwater anchor points limit precise operations such as welding, object manipulation, and sample collection. To achieve the goal of both swimming and walking on the benthic surface for heightened mobility, a bio-inspired solution based on crab locomotion is studied. We hypothesize that bio-inspired figure-8 gaits combined with a crab-like hexapod robot is a capable solution for swimming and walking on the benthic surface to a target location. To our knowledge, the presented robot is the first crab-like hexapod robot capable of autonomous, bio-inspired swimming, landing, and walking. A simulated model of the robot using MuJoCo is used to determine optimal gait paths, and the gaits are verified through experimental results for both walking and swimming. Preliminary testing reproduced simulated results of swimming within 27% and walking within 26%. From these results, the work suggests that a bio-inspired strategy for moving from water to benthic environments is a feasible solution for underwater tasks. Lastly, modifying generated gait paths and a modular mechanical design philosophy leaves room for future optimization in locomotion and hydrodynamics.

title: Safe Bilateral Teleoperation of Multi-Agent Systems With Distributed Average Estimation
abstract: This work presents a bilateral teleoperation framework for multi-agent systems (MAS) operating over switching, weight-unbalanced communication networks. Commanding a swarm agent-by-agent does not scale, and realistic inter-robot networks are directed, weight-unbalanced, and time-varying, with the single agent bridging the swarm to the human operator changing dynamically. To address this, every agent runs a modified PI-consensus estimator that recovers the operator's desired signal, and a new average estimator combining the push-sum algorithm with PI consensus to recover the swarm's true average reference. Unlike prior push-sum-based methods, this estimator's convergence is proven independent of both the number of agents and its own initial condition, under a strongly connected, weight-unbalanced, switching graph; boundedness and exact convergence of the individual and aggregate estimation errors are established via Lyapunov-based and input-output stability arguments. Building on these estimates, two abstracted tasks — average velocity and formation scaling — let a single master device intuitively drive the whole swarm's translation and shape without commanding individual agents. The resulting nominal command then passes through a per-agent control barrier function (CBF)-based quadratic program that finds the least-invasive input satisfying a forward-invariance safety constraint, guaranteeing collision-free operation with obstacles and other agents while deviating from operator intent only when necessary. Two complementary haptic feedback channels close the loop: a translating feedback proportional to the gap between nominal and achieved velocity, and a formation feedback proportional to formation-scale error, letting the operator feel both command feasibility and formation status. The framework is validated in simulation and hardware. In simulation, six agents reshape their formation to safely cross a field of two obstacle clusters, with both haptic signals showing clear transients during the avoidance maneuver before relaxing to zero once clear. In hardware, four quadrotors encircle and transport a spherical target via a bimanual haptic interface; a brief operator error near the 42-second mark disrupted the encirclement, yet the haptic cues alone — without visual feedback of the target — let the operator sense the deviation and restore formation, confirming real-world feasibility and the practical value of the proposed two-channel haptic design for operator guidance.

title: A Wearable Hand Exoskeleton with ML-Based Proportional Grip Force Control from EMG
abstract: Most wrist and hand exoskeletons are designed for clinical rehabilitation, leaving continuous, everyday grip assistance largely unaddressed. We present an open-source, tendon-driven hand exoskeleton with independently actuated 3-DOF thumb control and machine-learning-based proportional grip force control from surface electromyography (sEMG). The system enables continuous, muscle-driven modulation of grip strength rather than discrete gesture classification or threshold-gated actuation. An 8-channel, 500 Hz sEMG armband provides a 107-dimensional feature set comprising time-domain, frequency-domain, and cross-channel features to a machine learning regression model that estimates grip force in real time. Four regression architectures, XGBoost, support vector regression, random forest, and gradient boosting, were benchmarked using 5-fold cross-validation grouped by calibration trial to prevent window-level data leakage. XGBoost matched the highest offline accuracy (R² = 0.962) while training 6-7 times faster than random forest and gradient boosting, facilitating rapid per-user recalibration. Across 10 able-bodied participants, the deployed controller achieved real-time filtered performance of R² = 0.918 (NRMSE = 8.2%, r = 0.976) against synchronously measured ground-truth grip force, with predictions leading measured force by a mean of 173 ms. In a separate pilot assessment, the exoskeleton was evaluated on an individual with spinal cord injury (SCI), comparing hand range of motion with and without device assistance; the exoskeleton increased the participant's overall hand range of motion from 12.2% to 60.8% of the unimpaired reference range. Independently, the device's own actuation was characterized to deliver up to 13 N of grip force (peak 17 N) and 3.3 N of pinch force (peak 4.7 N) with no user effort applied. Representative trials illustrate the underlying signal quality: for the top-performing able-bodied participant, median-filtered predictions closely tracked measured force (R² = 0.983), while for the SCI participant, raw predictions were visibly noisier before the 7-window median filter recovered the underlying force trajectory (R² improving from 0.682 to 0.822). These results demonstrate that the proposed proportional sEMG control framework can be reliably calibrated and deployed across a heterogeneous multi-user cohort while maintaining accurate real-time grip force estimation. The SCI pilot further provides preliminary evidence of functional benefit, supporting the feasibility of continuous, EMG-driven proportional control for everyday assistive hand exoskeletons beyond the rehabilitation clinic.

title: Stiffness-Graded End-Effectors with Robust Adhesion using Dynamic Covalent Networks
abstract: Hybrid soft-rigid robots frequently fail not within their constituent materials but at the interfaces between them, where mismatched stiffness and poor adhesion drive delamination under repeated loading. Here, we present a simple synthesis method for dynamic covalent networks that addresses this problem directly through bond exchange at the network level, yielding both broadly tunable bulk mechanics and robust interfacial adhesion in a single material platform. By tuning network architecture, we program tensile moduli across three orders of magnitude (0.2–250 MPa), from compliant elastomers (strain at break >1000%) to rigid, load-bearing plastics (yield stress ~15 MPa). Notably, our elastomeric formulations do not require solvents or air-free synthesis and are readily shaped via compression molding or direct resin casting, enabling straightforward prototyping and potential for scale-up. At thermally bonded soft-stiff interfaces, T-peel testing shows our dynamic network pairings fail cohesively and endure ~10x greater stress at failure than a control pairing made with a commercial thermoset elastomer and thermoplastic, which instead delaminates adhesively. We demonstrate the robotic utility of this materials platform by fabricating stiffness-graded end-effectors for crab-inspired robots with embedded tactile sensing functionality via a compliant Hall-effect sensor. Softer elastomer formulations within the compliant sensing mechanism improved tactile sensitivity but introduced viscoelastic hysteresis, revealing a sensitivity-response trade-off relevant to future sensor design. Overall, this material platform offers a scalable route to robotic structures with durable, adhesive-free bonding at soft-rigid interfaces.

title: Safe Robot CBF Control with Scalable Soft Skins
abstract: Safe physical interaction requires both practical whole-body contact sensing and a controller that can use that contact information directly. We present a custom-molded soft pneumatic skin with a straightforward manufacturing process designed to make whole-body robot coverage practical, together with a safety-control module that uses measured skin indentation as a control barrier function (CBF) constraint. The silicone skin is injection molded using a custom 3D-printed mold and integrated on link 5 of a Franka FR3. title: Do Rigid-Body Simulators Dream of Soft Robots? Learning Contact-Rich Manipulation for Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots
abstract: Learning contact-rich, whole-body manipulation for soft continuum robots is held back by the lack of simulation infrastructure that has accelerated rigid-robot manipulation. Existing soft robot simulators are physically grounded but lack the contact handling, actuation support, or learning integration needed for contact-rich manipulation; rigid-body approximations offer these capabilities but sacrifice physical grounding. We bridge this gap for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) by deriving a continuum-mechanics-informed discretization that places the soft robot natively inside MuJoCo, unifying tendon forces, body contact, and dynamics in a single physics pipeline. We validate the simulator against a Cosserat rod reference (static and dynamic) and real TDCR hardware. We then train state-based imitation learning policies via teleoperation in simulation and deploy them zero-shot to a physical 3-segment TDCR on a 7-DoF Franka arm across two contact-rich manipulation tasks. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of sim-to-real transfer for contact-rich manipulation with continuum robots.

title: From Conversation to Execution: Learning through instruction and dialog for Robots in Safety-Critical Environments.
abstract: Teaching robots new procedural tasks remains a persistent challenge. Manual programming requires engineering effort for every task, learning from demonstration requires many physical examples, and policies trained on large datasets are opaque and difficult to verify, a serious limitation in safety-critical settings. We address this challenge with dialog-based script learning grounded entirely in symbolic, interpreted knowledge. Scripts describe complex events with component subevents, and ontologically grounded agents use them to represent the procedural knowledge necessary to execute complex tasks. In our system, an agent configured in an ontologically grounded cognitive architecture operates within HARMONIC, a cognitive robotic architecture, and learns a complete, executable task script from a single natural-language walkthrough given by a human teammate, with no training data, no reward tuning, and no statistical approximation of meaning. The teammate's utterances are translated into ontologically grounded meaning representations over which all reasoning is carried out. The learning procedure is itself encoded declaratively as a metascript in the agent's ontology, describing the sequence of events the agent undertakes when learning. This includes recognizing a teaching intent, selecting a learning target, normalizing and ordering the event sequence, extracting preconditions, and incorporating the finished script and associated lexicon entries into the agent's knowledge resources, at which point it is immediately executable. The approach is domain-independent, operating over a large lexicon and ontology rather than a narrow vocabulary, and every stage of learning and every piece of learned knowledge can be read, checked, and corrected by a human, a property valuable for safety-critical human-robot teaming. We demonstrate the metascript by tracing how a robot learns to replace a fuse through dialog with a human partner and then executes the task in a simulated ship engine room.

title: When Prediction Becomes Noise: Timing Multimodal Feedback for Robotic Scrub Nurses
abstract: Predictive robotic scrub nurses can prepare instruments before an explicit request. However, providing prediction information at the wrong time may interrupt clinicians rather than support coordination. We conducted a Wizard-of-Oz study of a multimodal robotic scrub nurse interface with 13 participants. Participants performed a visually demanding task while requesting instruments under four scenarios: normal recognition, misrecognition, detection failure, and prediction mismatch. Voice feedback supported error detection and recovery when provided during an active request. All participants immediately corrected misrecognized commands, and participants promptly switched to manual control following detection failures. In contrast, 3 participants did not immediately notice or correct a prediction mismatch announced before a request. Participants also described repeated prediction announcements as distracting or unnecessary. These findings indicate that voice feedback should focus on request confirmation, task completion, and error recovery, while predictions and system state should remain available through a graphical interface. The results show that the value of robot feedback depends not only on what information is provided, but also on when and how it is presented.

title: A Centralized MPC Framework for Safe Rendezvous with Nonholonomic, Curvature-Constrained Unmanned Ground Vehicles
abstract: This work presents a centralized Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework for safe rendezvous of nonholonomic, curvature-constrained unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs). In practical applications, teams of UGVs may need to rendezvous at a spontaneously determined location while achieving a desired final formation orientation and velocity, respecting vehicle curvature and actuation constraints, and avoiding collisions with neighboring vehicles and environmental obstacles. However, existing solutions in the literature address these requirements only partially and, in particular, solutions considering curvature-constrained nonholonomic UGVs are very scarce. To address these research gaps with a solution that can handle the aforementioned practical requirements simultaneously, we propose a framework that combines a multi-objective MPC formulation with discrete higher-order Control Barrier Function constraints to generate coordinated, safe trajectories for the UGV team. The developed controller can successfully compute the optimal rendezvous location and formation configuration, satisfying the desired properties, such as final orientation and formation velocity upon convergence. The proposed solution is evaluated against an existing rendezvous method for curvature-constrained vehicles under identical initial conditions and vehicle and formation parameters. For the team of 6 UGVs considered, our method achieves final position and orientation alignment while reducing rendezvous time from approximately 335s for the benchmark to less than 60s. Additional results with the controller, demonstrating UGV team to rendezvous in motion, while successfully avoiding static environmental obstacles, are also included. Furthermore, the scalability of the proposed method, in terms of computation times and solver success rates, with the number of UGVs in the formation has been analyzed quantitatively via Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, the future directions of this effort have been specified.

title: Informative Gaits for Detecting Buried Metallic Objects with Legged Robots
abstract: This research aims to develop and characterize walking gaits for crab-inspired robots with Hall effect-based compliance sensors that maximize probing search capabilities for metallic objects buried in sand. We develop gaits that increase the horizontal search space the legs cover during swing compared to a baseline gait. A dataset of sensor measurements is collected by allowing the robot to interact with metallic rods buried at various depths in sand. A metric is developed to assess variations in measurements due to interactions with the rods and compare gait performance. The results show that the developed gaits can outperform the baseline gait for objects buried at depths greater than 2 cm, exhibiting tradeoffs at different depths.

title: Redesigning a Crab-Like Robot for Surf Zone Operations
abstract: Shallow surf zones present a challenging environment for unexploded ordnance (UXO) search and retrieval due to loose granular media, uneven terrain, and dynamic coastal conditions. This work presents an 18-DOF amphibious crab-inspired robotic platform for UXO search and retrieval in these environments. Building upon a previous platform, the robot was redesigned to improve reliability and mobility using direct-drive actuators, redesigned dactyls, a waterproof electronics enclosure, and an updated ROS-based control system. Initial field testing demonstrated stable forward and lateral locomotion on both level and sloped beach terrain, validating the redesigned mechanical and electrical systems.

title: AeRove: A Lightweight Hybrid Aerial-Terrestrial Drone for Autonomous Pipeline Inspection
abstract: Inspection of pipelines for damage, gas leaks, and corrosion remains challenging due to confined geometries and the need to minimize human exposure to hazardous environments. This work presents AeRove, a lightweight hybrid robotic system that combines aerial and terrestrial locomotion within a single compact platform by converting its propeller guards into wheels, enabling a 200-millisecond transition between flight and ground traversal. Weighing 130 grams, AeRove is small enough to traverse pipelines of varying diameters, and its modular architecture allows adaptation to other applications through simple mechanical substitution. Low-level control and sensing run onboard, while higher-level autonomy and data processing are handled by a Wi-Fi-connected base station. This work establishes an adaptable, scalable method for pipeline inspection.

title: PC-VLA: A Sub-Million Parameter Predictive-Coding Policy for Language-Conditioned Robot Manipulation
abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance in robotic manipulation, but often rely on billions of parameters and large-scale robot pretraining. We introduce PC-VLA, a compact predictive-coding policy for language-conditioned robot manipulation that achieves competitive performance without large-scale robot pretraining. PC-VLA combines a frozen visual-language frontend with a lightweight 0.676M-parameter trainable recurrent policy. The recurrent hierarchy jointly predicts visual observations, proprioceptive states, and actions, while online error regression continuously updates the internal latent trajectory using sensory prediction errors. Hierarchical recurrent layers operating at different time scales capture both slow task-level structure and fast motor dynamics. We evaluate PC-VLA on LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-Object using 14 independently trained seeds and 50 rollouts per task. PC-VLA achieves an average success rate of 86.8%, while substantially outperforming parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM behavior-cloning baselines. Ablation studies further show that hierarchical temporal structure and online latent-state inference are critical to performance. These results suggest that predictive and hierarchical architectures with online inference provide a parameter-efficient alternative to scaling model size and robot pretraining data for language-conditioned robot manipulation.

title: Foot shape matters in sand: How redesigning crab-like dactyls increases walking speed for amphibious crab robot
abstract: Legged robots experience sinkage and slip in granular media that hinders forward progress, reducing locomotion speed and efficiency. This work characterizes the locomotion performances of several dactyl (end-effector) geometries on an 18-DOF hexapod robot. The design with the largest step sizes in two different walking modes in both dry and submerged sand was an X-shaped dactyl consisting of four fins. This X-shaped dactyl design was modeled in a MuJoCo sand simulation implementing granular resistive force theory (RFT) with rings of varying sizes and heights attached to determine an optimal placement to limit servo torque throughout the step and to maintain penetration depth. All designs were experimentally evaluated in dry sand and sand submerged in water for both forward and sideways walking gaits. The final X-shaped dactyl with embedded rings increased the average step size across all four walking modes by over 400% compared to the initial pronged dactyl design. These results were determined to be statistically significant (p<0.05) using Dunn's post hoc test. The results demonstrate that increasing interaction area and limiting excessive penetration are effective strategies for improving locomotion speed and efficiency in granular media. Additionally, this approach demonstrates how RFT-based optimizations improve locomotion performance for robots operating on granular surfaces.

title: Effect Of Motion Scaling On A Soft Continuum Robot Target-Reaching Task
abstract: Soft robots offer compliant and adaptable motion, but these same properties can make their behavior difficult to predict and control during human operation. Motion scaling directly affects how quickly operator inputs produce robot motion and may therefore influence task performance and user interaction. In this work, we investigate how motion scaling affects human performance during a target-reaching task with a pneumatically actuated soft continuum robot. Participants operate the robot under three within-participant conditions: fixed, user-adjusted, and automatic motion scaling. Performance is evaluated using trial completion, path efficiency, and subjective measures. Preliminary data have been collected from three participants. Preliminary results suggest that the automatic condition reduces perceived workload, while the user-adjusted condition appears to increase mental demand.

title: Leveraging Augmented Reality to Bridge the Sim2Real Gap in Robotic Movement Visualization
abstract: This research focuses on enhancing the visualization of planning and executing robot movement in an intuitive and understandable way for humans, aiming to contribute a more coherent form of communication for human-robot interaction and bridge the gap between simulation to reality by bringing simulation overlayed into reality. We aim to develop a web-based interface that utilizes augmented reality (AR) for a Meta Quest headset application. We aim to provide users with comprehensible information regarding the robot's plan and projected movements to complete typical household chores. We describe our approach of connecting out an external camera device to our robotic system, implementing object detection and localization, and visualizing planned robot movements in preparation for execution through our web-based interface. Using our interface, the user is presented with overlayed trajectory information of the movement path that the robot plans to execute from an external point of view other than the robot's to allow for more environmental awareness. This work has great potential impact on furthering human-robot interaction, especially in shared tasks, for domestic robots by improving robot-to-user communication.

title: Autonomous Monocular Endoscopic Resection of Central Airway Obstruction
abstract: We present an autonomous, model-based framework for central airway tumor resection using the Virtuoso Endoscopic System (VES). Intraoperative tumor and airway geometry are recovered from monocular endoscopic video using either Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) or Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE), fit with a cylindrical harmonic surface model, and converted into progressive, margin-controlled electrocautery trajectories. Trajectories execute either open-loop, using VES forward kinematics, or closed-loop, using image-based visual servoing. We further introduce a combined strategy that initially scales MDE to SLAM and adaptively switches between open-loop and closed-loop modes. Across matched ex vivo trials, the combined method achieved the lowest cut-surface error of any individual configuration (1.27 +- 0.10 mm) and the second-highest tumor volume removal (72.2 +- 22.6%). These results indicate that geometry-aware, perception-driven autonomy can reliably meet clinical margin-deviation criteria in a realistic, enclosed-airway surgical setting.

title: Task Orchestration for Hospital Humanoid Robots: Field-Derived Constraints and Interface Design
abstract: Robot interfaces for hospitals largely remain within a direct control paradigm that does not match how clinical staff conceptualize their work. From a three-day field study with 15 stakeholders at a university hospital, we find that delegable scope is determined not only by robotic capability, but also by four additional conditions: the consequences of exception handling failure, command authority and the cost of confirmation, fit with deployment context, and regulatory requirements. We present NAMI.I, a tablet interface through which nurses compose delivery, collection, patrol, and guidance as clinical work units rather than robot commands, and decompose each task into its required execution capabilities and completion criteria. We close with open questions on confirmation-requiring execution, semantic goal recovery, and scheduling under heterogeneous temporal constraints.

title: Emphasis in the Stillness: Analysis of Perceived Pauses Around a Library of Canonical Postures, from Ballet to Robots in Human-facing Environments
abstract: What gives structure to a dancer’s grace? Human bodies are in constant motion; yet people perceive structure: phrasing and pauses (akin to periods at the end of sentences). This report proposes a system to endow robotic motion with similar features. Focusing on the charismatic structure of formalized dance (classical ballet), authors use a body movement annotation system to capture moments of perceived stillness for a corpus of 8 videos. Analyzing these videos reveals a key movement signature of slowing down a ~1.2 SD drop in joint-rotation speed) and quickly speeding back up after the “pause” (returning to baseline within ~0.5 s). However, other moments in the corpus also have this signature and were not flagged during annotation. This difference is explained by creating a library of key poses, named and frequently used in the classical ballet style, and measuring the distance of the posture in the annotated pause to the examples in this library. With this addition, we discriminate perceived pauses from equally slow non-pauses: at annotated pauses the body sits significantly closer to a canonical posture than at speed-matched control frames (paired test, p = 0.047). This explanatory analysis suggests that endowing robotic motion with key moments where movement slows and then sharply speeds up around a library of important postures could endow these systems with a similar sense of phrasing and grace.

title: Exploring Soft Continuum Robot Capabilities Through Control Theory and Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Soft continuum robots are highly underactuated and redundant, which makes control difficult due to limited control authority and weak stability guarantees. In this work, we show empirically that even for a simple trajectory-tracking task, PD- and Quadratic Program(QP)-PD-based task-space controllers can fail as the level of underactuation increases: without an inherent stability and convergence guarantee, these methods can map a desired task-space acceleration onto an infeasible joint-space acceleration. To actively enforce stability in the task-space error dynamics while respecting actuator constraints, we introduce a Soft Inverse Dynamics Control Lyapunov Function-based Quadratic Program (Soft ID-CLF_x0002_QP) tailored to highly underactuated soft robots. Experimental results demonstrate superior set-point and trajectory-tracking accuracy alongside consistent Lyapunov convergence compared to baseline methods. Furthermore, to handle contact-rich tasks where soft robot physics are difficult to model, such as object manipulation, we deploy an LSTM-based Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning policy in a partially observable setting. Preliminary simulation and sim_x0002_to-real hardware experiments show high-quality sweeping and grasping performance.

title: Black Boxes: An Educational Platform for Choreobotics
abstract: The growing intersection of dance and robotics (choreobotics) requires new tools for robotics education. These tools should foreground bodily expression, enabling students to focus their time and energy on movement design and contextual settings. This report presents an open-source prototype to address these needs. The system includes the design of a physical enclosure for an Arduino-based system of four servo motors controlled by four knobs in two distinct modes. A pilot educational experience was offered to two students without prior experience, one middle-school aged and one high-school aged, demonstrating the flexibility of the platform for different experience levels. These two students were given a symbol-based dance class to design their movements, created artificial bodies with pipe cleaners, and used the novel system to animate motion during a 6-hour course. Both achieved creative motion designs and embedded their movements in related environments, demonstrating a platform that makes the body-to-machine abstraction gap concrete and explorable.

title: Behavior is a Language for Cross-Embodiment Control
abstract: Behavior cloning (BC) models demonstrations as a sequence prediction problem often conditioned on a goal state, to reap the stability and performance benefits of supervised learning. Learning robot affordances by observing humans is generally a good idea since humans often act in near-optimal ways. However, robotic agents historically suffer from an embodiment problem. That is, an algorithm cannot simultaneously control all robotic systems; it becomes overfitted to the robot hardware, or embodiment, used in training. This creates additional challenges when learning from human experience as humans and robots have different bodies. This work presents BeLa, a flexible model that learns robot behavior from human examples. BeLa's design is based on the Perciever-IO transformer~cite{perceiverio}. This allows the model to attend to varying input/output sizes without adjustments. We hypothesize that this (1) helps to facilitate model reuse and (2) allows the model to benefit from broader pretraining than could be done with VLA that use action heads.

title: Heat-based Direct Ink Writing for Soft Magnetic Robot Fabrication
abstract: Soft magnetic robots are flexible robots composed of soft polymers or elastomers embedded with magnetic particles, enabling magnetic actuation in an external magnetic field. Due to their flexibility and scalability, soft magnetic robots have gained attention across various fields, including biomedicine, and electronics, where their properties and structures can be modified and utilized to facilitate exploration in complex, confined spaces. To fabricate magnetic soft robots, magnetic anisotropy is critical, enabling the programming of distinct particle orientations and yielding the unique multifunctional shape of soft magnetic robots. In this study we present and compare two common methods of programming soft robots during printing to identify which method maximizes magnetic remanence, therefore, robot bending. These configurations are extruding material over a permanent magnet and using an electromagnetic coil attached to the extruder tip. For this project, a direct ink writing additive manufacturing system was developed, including a custom non-magnetic bed support and syringe extruder, attached to the end-effector of a UR10e robotic arm. The magnetic ink used is a mixture of strontium ferrite microparticles mixed with EcoFlex 00-30 silicone elastomer. Magnetic characterization was performed using a vibrating sample magnetometer. Magnetic characterization showed that the sample printed over the permanent magnet presented the highest remanent magnetization, measured along its magnetization direction, indicating that particle alignment is stronger in this printing configuration. The control printing, with no magnetization, showed a similar profile to the simply poured sample, indicating that the extruding process alone does not significantly affect the magnetic properties of the printed material.

title: Toward Vision-Guided Terrain-Adaptive Locomotion in a Sea Turtle-Inspired Robot
abstract: Autonomous terrain-adaptive locomotion in low- profile, bio-inspired robots relies on onboard perception, yet near- ground clearance introduces severe optical bottlenecks. While sensor placement and viewpoint selection are well studied in mobile robotics, prior work largely focuses on taller quadrupeds, humanoids, and rovers rather than low-profile crawlers. As a result, grazing-angle views and texture foreshortening remain challenging for near-ground terrain sensing. This work presents an onboard vision-based terrain-recognition framework for a sea turtle-inspired robot. A MobileNetV2 classifier is trained on GTOS-Mobile imagery remapped into seven locomotion-relevant classes and adapted to the robot-camera domain using session- separated fine-tuning. Aspect-ratio-preserving letterboxing re- tains the complete camera field of view. The classifier is deployed on a Raspberry Pi 5 and integrated with the robot’s Central Pattern Generator (CPG) architecture, using terrain estimates to inform locomotion-mode selection. On 710 robot images from nine held-out sessions, fine-tuning increased accuracy from 52.39% to 83.10% and macro F1-score from 46.78% to 83.11%. Remaining errors were concentrated at the sand–solid-ground boundary, with 104 of 154 solid-ground images classified as sand. These results validate the hardware perception-to-CPG interface and motivate improved camera placement for closed-loop, vision- triggered gait adaptation.

title: Slow Thinking, Fast Safe Control: A Modular Alternative to End-to-End Vision-Language-Action
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated impressive semantic generalization for robotic manipulation, but they typically couple perception, reasoning, and low-level action prediction within a single learned policy [1,2]. This makes it difficult to impose explicit runtime safety constraints and creates a mismatch between the relatively slow rate of vision-language reasoning and the fast feedback required for safety-critical control. Sampling-based controllers such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control [3] and related approaches, such as Ensemble Kalman Inversion [4], provide fast closed-loop optimization but require that objectives, priors, and constraints be specified. Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide an explicit mechanism for runtime safety enforcement [5], yet do not determine task intent or how the robot should recover when a nominal action becomes unsafe. We present Slow Thinking, Fast Safe Control, a modular architecture that separates semantic reasoning, dynamic control, and runtime safety across complementary time scales. A vision-language model reasons over language instructions and multi-view visual observations to identify task-relevant objects, semantic constraints, subgoals, and route information. These outputs are compiled into objectives for an MPPI controller, which generates fast closed-loop actions, while a CBF layer projects nominal actions onto a constraint-satisfying set using robot-, obstacle-, and language-conditioned safety constraints. We evaluate the approach in MuJoCo on six manipulation challenges: obstacle pick-and-place, dynamic-obstacle transport, narrow-passage carrying, semantic keep-out, blocked-path recovery, and occluded-clutter retrieval. We compare SmolVLA, SmolVLA-CBF, and our VLM-MPPI-CBF architecture. SmolVLA uses a 450M-parameter policy with 99.9M fine-tuned parameters, trained on 128 demonstrations for 20k steps, while our method uses a frozen 3.75B-parameter Qwen2.5-VL model for semantic reasoning. In preliminary experiments, VLM-MPPI-CBF achieves 70% safe task success, compared with 13% for SmolVLA and 9% for SmolVLA-CBF. Our method exceeds 78% task success on five of six tasks and achieves 28% on the hardest task. These results suggest that explicit safety filtering alone cannot compensate for weak task execution, while separating semantic reasoning, fast model-based control, and runtime safety provides a promising direction for safer language-conditioned manipulation. title: Information-Aware Collaboration in Heterogeneous Micro-UAV Teams for Indoor Monitoring
abstract: Indoor monitoring requires robots to continuously acquire and update environmental information as conditions change. Existing multi-robot systems mainly coordinate motion, coverage, or task execution. The observations themselves are often treated as sensing outputs rather than a shared resource that guides future actions. This work presents an Information-Aware Collaboration (IAC) framework for heterogeneous micro-UAV teams. The framework identifies what information is needed next and selects the sensing platform best suited to acquire it. Environmental observations are maintained in a shared multimodal information field that captures freshness, environmental estimates, sensing modality, and information requirement. New observations are exchanged across the team and used to guide subsequent sensing decisions. Preliminary hardware tests with Crazyflie platforms using Flow Deck and Multi-ranger Deck modules, together with PyBullet-Gym simulations, support the feasibility of lightweight heterogeneous sensing for indoor monitoring.
