title: Pathways Into Robotics Research: A 13-Year Outcomes Analysis of Access and Graduate-School Continuation in an AI/Robotics REU
abstract: There is a persistent gap in robotics between students who receive research training and those who ultimately pursue research careers. Undergraduate research experiences (REUs) are an important mechanism for narrowing this gap, yet evidence of their effectiveness often relies on single-cohort, self-reported surveys of participants’ intentions rather than longitudinal evidence of their subsequent educational and career trajectories [1], [4]. In this work, we present a preliminary outcomes analysis of the Carnegie Mellon Robotics Institute Summer Scholars (RISS) program, drawing on longitudinal data from 13 cohorts spanning 2012–2025 (N = 547) collected through an internal alumni-tracking database. By examining participants’ observed post-program outcomes rather than relying solely on retrospective self-reporting, we establish a baseline for understanding longer-term outcomes associated with undergraduate robotics research experiences. This analysis also provides a foundation for developing a research-identity and belonging tool for future RISS cohorts, enabling future work to connect participants’ reported experiences during the program with their subsequent educational and career outcomes.

title: Intelligent Mobile Robot with Person Following and Fall Detection
abstract: This paper presents a compact indoor assistive-robot architecture that couples person following, skeleton-based fall detection, and map-aware navigation. A wheeled platform carries RGB and depth cameras: RGB frames drive detection, tracking, pose estimation, and spatio-temporal action recognition, while depth provides metric target range and supports RGB-D simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). The perception prototype uses the PP-Human pipeline with HRNet keypoints and an ST-GCN classifier. On a six-clip proof-of-concept subset of the UR Fall Detection dataset, all three fall clips triggered an alert and none of the three normal clips produced a false alert; the mean first-alert time was 5.07~s from clip start. These results validate integration feasibility rather than population-level accuracy. The proposed navigation layer converts the tracked person's depth into a map-frame goal and plans around static furniture while maintaining a reasonable following distance.

title: The CM Brushed Interface Board and Brushed Auxiliary Board: A Compact Modular System for Wearable Robotics
abstract: Wearable robotic technologies require embedded systems that are compact, robust, and computationally capable. However, existing wearable robotic hardware often compromises real-world usability through off-board electronics that are platform-specific, which restricts broader adoption. This work presents a modular embedded system stack, which is built around a production-ready single-board computer (Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, Raspberry Pi, Cambridge, UK). It contains two custom printed circuit boards: the CM Brushed Interface Board and the Brushed Auxiliary Board. Developed for the Variable Stiffness Orthosis in the Neurobionics Lab, the CM Brushed Interface Board comprises a motor driver and quadrature encoder counter, inertial measurement unit, 16-bit analog-to-digital converter, and power management, all within a small footprint. The optional Brushed Auxiliary Board attaches on top of the CM Brushed Interface Board and extends its functionality through the addition of a secondary motor driver and encoder counter, SD card reader, and barometric pressure sensor. Together, these boards co-locate all electronics in a package able to be distally mounted, eliminating the need for a remote waist pack and extending the quality, robustness, and size of research-grade embedded solutions. Integrated with an open-source software development kit, this embedded stack offers a portable, extensible foundation that lowers the barrier to prototyping across mechanically distinct wearable robotic systems.

title: Lightweight 3D-Aware Navigation for Tiny Drones in Dynamic Mapless Environments
abstract: Autonomous navigation for micro aerial vehicles is challenging under strict memory, compute, and energy constraints. Due to their small size, such platforms need lightweight sensors and embedded processors. While some lightweight approaches operate only in 2D, they are insufficient for aerial robots that move in 3D. However, most 3D-aware methods rely on volumetric voxel maps, SLAM pipelines, or GPU-class processors, making them unsuitable for resource-constrained embedded platforms. This paper presents a lightweight onboard 3D-aware navigation framework for a Crazyflie 2.1 with a GAP8-based AI-Deck. The system combines quantized monocular depth estimation, multi-ranger sensing, and incremental A* planning for dynamic, mapless environments. By separating horizontal local-map planning from vertical depth-based reasoning, the approach enables 3D-aware navigation without volumetric voxel maps or 3D pose estimation. The complete pipeline runs onboard within the GAP8's 64 KB L1 and 512 KB L2 memory constraints.

title: Distributed 3D Leader–Follower Formation Control with Field-of-View Safety via Control Barrier Functions
abstract: This extended abstract presents a distributed perception-aware control framework for three-dimensional leader--follower formation (3D-LFF) of multi-UAV systems with limited onboard sensing. The key challenge is that a follower may satisfy its formation objective while simultaneously driving the leader outside the camera field of view (FOV) or usable depth range, causing loss of relative-state observability. We formulate the leader pose relative to the follower camera using distance, azimuth, elevation, and relative heading, derive corresponding 3D-LFF kinematics, and design a distributed formation controller using local relative states and the leader's communicated velocity. A Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program (CBF-QP) minimally modifies the nominal command whenever needed to enforce the full camera-frustum constraints. Gazebo simulations and Crazyflie hardware experiments show that the nominal controller tracks the desired formation when safety constraints are inactive, while the CBF-QP preserves visibility during conflicting formation commands and abrupt leader motion.

title: Learning Differentiable Control Barrier Functions for Real-Time Safe Autonomy
abstract: This work introduces a learning-based approach for the numerical construction of control barrier functions (CBFs). The approach leverages the dynamic backup CBF framework to compute the CBF values over a given mesh. The collected data is then used to train a neural network that approximates both the CBF and its gradient. It is shown that tigtening the constraints with a safety margin can mitigate approximation errors at the safety boundary, suggesting a viable method of constructing computationally lightweight safe controllers for real-time robotic systems.

title: Gaze-Aware VLMs for Object Grounding in Human-Robot Interaction
abstract: In embodied human-robot interaction, people often refer to objects with underspecified language and behavioral cues such as gaze, for example saying ""clean that"" while looking at a vase. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read such behavior from images but cannot directly use the precise gaze direction a robot's sensors record. We study how to feed gaze directly into a VLM's input for object grounding, in three stages. Because the source interaction data contain no images, we first reconstruct the scenes in a virtual environment and render them from user, robot, and distributed viewpoints, and we train a gaze-alignment model that predicts when the user is attending to the target. Stage 1 then compares design choices in a fully crossed experiment: which camera view to use, whether to keep all frames or only the single predicted target-attended frame, and how to inject gaze (none, a visible marker on the frame, or patch-level feature weighting). Task-specific adaptation mattered most: the fine-tuned model outperformed both its untuned base and GPT-4o on target-related questions, and keeping the whole frame sequence beat using one frame. Gaze was not uniformly useful, since drawing it on every frame can hide the object and reduce accuracy on object type, color, and shape. Stage 2 therefore adopts a hybrid design that shows the gaze marker only on the predicted target-attended frame and leaves the rest of the clip untouched; it was the most balanced across question types, and no alternative significantly outperformed it. In Stage 3, a model adapted only on the virtual data improved on instructions collected in a real office, most clearly for relative position, which suggests that virtual reconstruction is a practical way to gather behavior-grounded interaction data.

title: MinTWorm: A Miniature Tensegrity Worm Robot for Multi-Terrain Locomotion and Payload Transport
abstract: Miniature robots have recently attracted significant attention due to their potential for operating in confined and complex environments. However, these robots face technical challenges such as low reliability and maneuverability, as many of them still rely on mechanisms with low stiffness, fragile joints, or limited structural morphing capability. Tensegrity structures offer a promising solution because of their lightweight nature, high stiffness-to-weight ratio, and inherent reconfigurability, yet their application at the miniature robotic scale remains largely unexplored. To address this technical gap, this paper presents MinTWorm, a miniature tensegrity worm robot designed to investigate the feasibility of tensegrity structures for small-scale robotic systems. The robot body consists of four tensegrity unit cells, each based on a modified six-bar icosahedral tensegrity structure. Inspired by earthworm peristalsis, locomotion of MinTWorm is achieved through sequential contraction and deployment of the unit cells actuated by shape memory alloy actuators. Experimental results show that MinTWorm is currently the smallest and lightest worm-like tensegrity robot, being significantly smaller and lighter than existing designs. Its unit cells represent some of the smallest tensegrity modules reported to date. The robot demonstrates adaptable locomotion across diverse terrains, including open surface, narrow pathway, loose sand, unsteady rock surface, and vertical tube. Furthermore, MinTWorm is capable of transporting payloads up to nearly six times its own body mass and performing payload offloading.

title: AssistMoVE: A Simulation Toolkit for Mobility Evaluation of Physically Assistive Robots
abstract: Physically assistive robots must operate in everyday environments while maintaining mobility, stability, task feasibility, and user comfort. Specifically, for assistive mobility robots, such as robotic wheelchairs, this creates a need for reproducible, standard referenced simulation environments that capture everyday terrain, passage, and obstacle conditions that affect passability and ride quality. We present AssistMoVE, a feasibility and workflow demonstration of a simulation toolkit for generating daily-life mobility scenarios and testing robot mobility behavior in Isaac Sim. The toolkit combines parameterized benchmark scenes with a controller interface for mobile robot models through generated environments. Using the Robotic Assistive Mobility and Manipulation Platform (RAMMP) as a case study, we demonstrate a workflow from Computer-Aided Design (CAD)-to-Universal Scene Description (USD), scenario generation, controller setup, and passability testing. We further define quantitative-ready measures, including traversal success, platform orientation, and seat-frame acceleration, to support future human-centered evaluation of physically coupled mobility systems.

title: Path-Constrained Admittance Control for Human-Robot Interaction via Screw Theory
abstract: Numerous robot–environment interaction tasks require precise compliance control of the end-effector along a prescribed fixed path. This path may be defined in Cartesian space, involving only the end-effector position; in SO(3), involving only the end-effector orientation; or in SE(3), involving both position and orientation. Existing Cartesian-space impedance and admittance control approaches typically treat translational and rotational motions independently, thereby failing to capture the intrinsic coupling between position and orientation in tasks naturally defined in SE(3). Consequently, an interaction control framework that explicitly accounts for this coupling is essential. In this paper, we propose a unified screw-theory-based framework for admittance control of robot manipulators along arbitrary constrained paths, regardless of whether the translational and rotational motions are coupled or decoupled.

title: Beyond Walking–Sensorized Multifunctional Legs for Clearing Granular Media
abstract: We present a 14 degree of freedom underwater hexapod robotic platform which utilizes legs for walking and clearing sand and debris from a buried object or area of interest. The middle leg on each side of the robot, used for cleaning, have three servo-driven joints. The end effectors of these legs contain integrated strain sensors consisting of a magnet and magnetometer separated by a flexible elastomer, similar in construction to those presented in [1]. The remaining four legs, used primarily for walking, have two degrees of freedom to reduce cost and complexity. The robot is tested cleaning the surface of a flat circular target buried in sand and gravel. While standing in place, it performs a series of outward swiping motions with one leg at increasing depth. The exposed area of the target after cleaning is measured via photography and computer vision. When the target is buried in 2-3cm of sand, the robot is able to clear an area of approximately 50 cm2 on average. In gravel, the cleared area averages 97 cm2. During these tests, the output of the integrated leg sensor is measured, revealing peaks each time the end effector scraped against the target. I future work, this sensor feedback will be used to detect contact with buried objects or changes in the substrate, informing autonomous cleaning behaviors. References [1] J. Grezmak and K. A. title: KOBRA-MPC: Convex MPC for Wheeled Mobile Robots via Analytical Koopman Bilinearization
abstract: Wheeled mobile robot (WMR) trajectory tracking is challenging because of nonlinear dynamics, nonholonomic constraints, and the intrinsic SE(2) geometry of the configuration space. Nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) can achieve accurate tracking but requires solving a nonconvex optimization problem at every sampling instant, limiting real-time applicability. Existing convex model predictive control (MPC) approaches are computationally attractive but often rely on local linearization and may not preserve the underlying WMR geometry. This work presents KOBRA-MPC, a convex model predictive control framework based on an analytically derived Koopman bilinear realization (KOBRA) of differential-drive WMR dynamics. Starting from physically interpretable geometric seed observables, we construct a countable Koopman dictionary and prove that its span is invariant under the Lie derivatives associated with the drift and input vector fields. This yields an exact infinite-dimensional Koopman bilinear representation that preserves the WMR’s SE(2) geometry and nonholonomic structure and admits a closed-form state reconstruction map. For practical implementation, we derive a finite-dimensional truncation and establish an explicit uniform bound on the resulting truncation approximation error. The residual is independent of the control input and converges to zero as the truncation order increases, while reconstruction of the physical state remains exact. Building on this finite-dimensional model, KOBRA-MPC evaluates the bilinear input matrix along a recursively updated guide trajectory, producing a linear time-varying prediction model. Consequently, each constrained receding-horizon optimal control problem is reduced to a convex quadratic program (QP). The main contributions are: (i) an analytical, geometry-preserving Koopman embedding for WMR dynamics with a provably invariant observable space; (ii) a finite-dimensional Koopman bilinear realization with an explicit, vanishing truncation-error bound and exact state reconstruction; (iii) a constrained convex MPC formulation that converts the bilinear lifted dynamics into an LTV model and avoids online nonlinear optimization; and (iv) cross-platform validation in PyBullet on Pioneer 3-DX and ROSbot XL robots and physical experiments on a TurtleBot3 Burger under indoor and outdoor conditions. Experiments show that KOBRA-MPC requires only 3.74–4.55 ms per MPC step in simulation, providing approximately 3× speedup over GMPC and 4.7–7.3× over NMPC. Physical experiments demonstrate tracking accuracy comparable to NMPC while being approximately 5–6.5× faster, together with substantially improved tracking over GMPC on challenging trajectories and robustness to outdoor surface-induced model mismatch. Videos to the experiments are avilable at https://kobrampcpaper.github.io/

title: Beyond the Fixed View: Registered XR Viewpoint Acquisition for Manipulation Recovery
abstract: When a manipulation attempt fails, the object is often left where the robot’s fixed camera can no longer measure it. Because occlusion depends on the object, gripper, and clutter configuration at the moment of failure, pre-placed sensors cannot be guaranteed to detect it. We address this post-failure observability problem by turning one human-selected extended-reality (XR) view into a robot-frame measurement. An operator captures an informative view with a Samsung Galaxy XR headset; independently surveyed wall markers register that image to a UR5e workcell. Across 17 trials spanning occlusion levels o = 0 to o = 1, fixed-camera localization error is strongly coupled to occlusion (r = 0.87, p < 10−4), rising from an 18 mm median when the target is clear to 148 mm when it is ambiguous, while error from the acquired viewpoint is not significantly related to occlusion (r = 0.40, p = 0.12) and stays between 32 and 41 mm. Notably, the fixed camera rarely fails by reporting nothing in 6 of the 14 trials in which it did report a pose that was over 40 mm from ground truth with no accompanying indication of degradation. Together, these findings provide a first step toward shared sensing and, ultimately, a shared cognitive state in which humans understand robot sensing limitations and robots incorporate human-provided observations during naturalistic collaboration.

title: Learning Expressive Humanoid Locomotion from Monocular Runway Videos for Robot Fashion Shows
abstract: Runway walking requires coordinated control of posture, stride, foot placement, and whole-body motion to effectively present clothing and convey a distinctive style. However, humanoid robots used in fashion shows typically rely on locomotion policies optimized primarily for stability and walking speed, limiting their ability to reproduce expressive, human-like runway motions. In this work, we present an end-to-end framework that transforms monocular runway videos into deployable humanoid locomotion policies through motion recovery, robot retargeting, motion correction, policy training, simulation-based evaluation, and physical deployment. We evaluate the proposed framework on the Booster K1 humanoid robot using runway-style catwalk motions. The learned policy completed every physical trial without falling, while reproducing the characteristic narrow foot placement and coordinated movement of the legs, torso, and arms. The results demonstrate that our proposed training framework enables the Booster K1 to perform stable and expressive catwalk motions, highlighting its potential for humanoid robotic applications in fashion shows and other performance-oriented scenarios.

title: DriveScene: A Comprehensive Video Dataset for Scenario Understanding, Generation, and Explanation in Autonomous Driving Research
abstract: Ensuring autonomous vehicles are trustworthy and transparent is crucial for safety and public trust, especially in high-stakes emergent scenarios. Existing driving datasets rarely capture safety-critical situations or provide the detailed annotations needed for explainable decision-making and human-centered scenario analysis. We introduce DriveScene, a large-scale ego-centric driving video dataset covering routine and emergent scenarios with annotations spanning scenario context, object-level grounding, and human-centered perception judgments. DriveScene contains 3,327 verified clips selected from 31,116 videos and aligns detailed scenario annotations with de-identified ratings and driving-related attributes collected from 408 participants. These rich annotations support important object identification, emergent video generation, explanation generation, and perceived-risk modeling.

title: Who Creates Agricultural Robots? Place-Conscious Pilots to Scale Community Participation in Robotics & AI R&D&D
abstract: Robotics, artificial intelligence (AI), and automation are transforming agriculture, yet a critical gap remains between the communities these technologies are intended to serve and the Research, Development, and Deployment (R&D&D) processes that shape them. Although rural communities comprise approximately 41% of the global population and possess substantial agricultural knowledge, they are often positioned as technology adopters rather than contributors to innovation. This study explores how place-conscious pathways can expand participation in agricultural robotics and AI R&D&D by engaging rural communities as contributors, co-creators, and future technology leaders. Building on a multi-year collaboration with rural Pennsylvania communities beginning in 2019, these are two pilot initiatives. The first, the FIRA Robotics Village, connected agricultural robotics companies, researchers, growers, students, and community members around technologies tailored to regional crops and farming systems. The second, PA Robotics & AI Scholars, created customized pathways within Carnegie Mellon University's Robotics Institute Summer Scholars (RISS) program for students from agricultural and rural backgrounds to participate in robotics and AI research. Results suggest that place-conscious engagement can shift participation beyond technology exposure toward meaningful contribution. The FIRA Robotics Village provided opportunities for community members and students to connect with innovators, encounter emerging technologies, and envision themselves as participants in agricultural innovation. PA Robotics & AI Scholars demonstrated how rural and agricultural students contribute valuable perspectives shaped by farming, rural life, and community experience. Across both pilots, participants contributed contextual knowledge, observations, and questions that may otherwise be absent from technology development processes. Together, the pilots suggest a progression from Explore → Participate → Grow → Contribute → Lead, representing a shift from workforce preparation toward capability creation, where communities gain the ability to interpret, shape, and influence technological change rather than simply respond to it. The findings indicate that rural communities are not only locations where agricultural robotics and AI will be deployed, but also sources of knowledge, innovation, future researchers, and future technology leaders. Future work will expand these pilots across additional agricultural contexts to examine how place-conscious pathways can be adapted to diverse communities and production systems while investigating long-term participant outcomes and mechanisms for integrating rural knowledge into robotics and AI R&D&D. Pennsylvania serves as an initial demonstration environment, with the broader goal of developing a framework for connecting community assets, local expertise, and agricultural innovation ecosystems.

title: Shape Reconstruction of Robot Swarms via Vibration-Based Contact Sensing and Wireless Communication
abstract: Knowing the internal geometry of GPS-denied environments like subsurface voids is critical for safety assessment and rescue operations, yet traditional sensor-based mapping tools fail where line-of-sight is obstructed. We propose an approach in which the contact topology of a homogeneous robot swarm is sufficient to recover the shape of the assembly and, by extension, the geometry of the space it fills without any ranging sensor, global positioning, or external infrastructure. To this end, we develop a system of robots called Vibration Circles, each equipped with both actuation and sensing capabilities: eccentric-mass motors serve as vibration actuators, and a 9-DOF IMU serves as the receiver, capturing the mechanical signal transmitted through physical contact. Each robot detects which neighbors it is touching by analyzing the vibration it receives when a neighbor's motors are active. For each pair of robots, we compute a symmetric coupling index that normalizes cross-node vibration energy by each robot's self-energy, making the metric robust to motor-to-motor amplitude variation. Thresholding this index yields a binary contact adjacency matrix, which is passed to a virtual-force localization algorithm that recovers robot center positions from contact information alone. We demonstrate the full pipeline in 2D on a 9-robot square formation tested across five independent assemblies, achieving correct adjacency classification in 68 of 72 node pairs and sub-millimeter position reconstruction error. The approach is designed to extend naturally to 3D with similar spherical robots.

title: Feel the Ground: Radar based Terrain Classification towards Gait Adaptation in Legged Robots
abstract: Legged robots operating outdoors must continually adapt their gait to changing terrain. Reliable terrain classification is therefore important for stable and efficient locomotion, particularly in unstructured environments where the terrain can change unexpectedly. Existing approaches generally rely on either exteroceptive or proprioceptive sensing, both of which have important limitations. Vision-based methods using cameras and LiDAR can perform well in controlled conditions, but their performance can degrade under low illumination, dust, fog, and occlusion. Proprioceptive methods based on IMU and joint encoder measurements are less affected by these conditions, but are inherently reactive: they provide information about the terrain only after the robot has made physical contact, limiting their ability to support anticipatory gait adaptation. mmWave radar provides a promising alternative for contact-free terrain sensing. Its backscattered signal contains information about the physical and dielectric properties of the surface, which are difficult to observe with optical sensors and can influence traction and traversability. At the same time, radar is largely unaffected by lighting and is more robust to common outdoor obscurants. This raises a natural question: can ground material be identified directly from sparse mmWave radar returns, before the robot makes contact? In this work, we investigate this question as a first step toward radar-informed gait adaptation. We make two con- tributions: (1) a cross-modal pipeline that generates radar material labels without manual annotation, and (2) a diag- nostic study that examines the radar signal chain to identify where a generalizable material signal is actually present.

title: Hierarchical Differentiable Co-Design of a Soft Pneumatic Leg and Robot Body for Shallow-Water Locomotion
abstract: Soft robotic swimmers at the air–water interface exhibit strong coupling among actuator deformation, appendage placement, body drag, buoyancy, environmental interactions, and control timing. Baseline experiments showed that a four-leg front–rear configuration at 45◦ reached 24.49 ± 2.48 mm/s despite not maximizing isolated-leg thrust. In vegetated water, leg–obstacle interactions reduced forward velocity and disrupted turning, particularly for the deeper-submerged 90◦ configuration. These results motivate morphology optimization beyond thrust alone. A differentiable CFD/FSI framework with free-form deformation (FFD) optimized robot-body morphology and reduced time-averaged drag by approximately 33% within 100 iterations. Future work will extend the framework to soft-leg cavity optimization for hierarchical actuator-to-robot co-design.

title: Model Agnostic Agentic Framework for Long-Horizon Robotic Navigation and Planning
abstract: General purpose robots must reason over users natural language instructions while navigating diverse environments and be able to perform long-horizon tasks. Recent Vision Language Action (VLA) models attempt to address this challenge using end-to-end policies, but often require substantial task, environment and embodiment specific training and remain unstable when deployed in unseen environments. In this work we present a modular framework that decouples high level reasoning from low level motion control by combining a Vision Language Model (VLM) with classical robotic navigation approaches. In our framework, a VLM performs task planning, task breakdown, grounded tool usage, and monitoring, while RTAB-Map and Nav2 provide mapping, localization, dynamic collision avoidance, and trajectory execution without the need for environment specific fine-tuning. To bridge semantic reasoning with motion control, we introduce point navigation and map navigation tools that ground VLM predictions into 3D navigation goals using RGB camera images, depth maps, camera parameters, and TF transformations. Further more the framework incorporates a monitoring mechanism that enables the VLM to detect unsafe and unintended behaviors and trigger replanning during execution. We evaluate the framework across multiple benchmarks, including a Behavior-1K based benchmark and VLN-CE Habitat environment benchmark designed to assess the frameworks navigation capabilities. Results demonstrate the ability of our proposed approach to combine the high level planning ability of VLMs with the reliability of classical planners, enabling long-horizon navigation without retraining for individual environments or robot embodiments.

title: Toward Study on the Effects of Robot's Humorous Apology on Human's Trust Recovery
abstract: Robot errors can disrupt human-robot collaboration by reducing user trust and willingness to rely on the robot. Robot apologies can support trust recovery after such errors, but their effects may vary with apology strategy and error severity. This study therefore presents a user experiment based on a 2×2 between-subjects factorial design to examine the effect of humorous robot apologies on user trust recovery and the moderating role of error severity. The design crosses robot error severity (low vs. high) with apology strategy (generic vs. humorous). An online experiment will be conducted using the open-source Warehouse Robot Interaction Simulator. Participants will complete a collaborative task, experience a robot error followed by an apology, and report trust, trust recovery, interaction experience and reuse intention. We hypothesize that humorous apologies will produce greater trust recovery than generic apologies after low-severity errors, but that the advantage of humor will weaken or reverse after high-severity errors.

title: Improved Postural Stability Using a Soft Semi-active Device Following a Forward Loss of Balance
abstract: Falls resulting from trip-like perturbations can cause serious injuries, motivating wearable devices that improve balance recovery. The trunk requires substantial biomechanical adjustments during recovery from a forward loss of balance, suggesting that back support devices (BSDs) that directly assist trunk extension may improve stability. For this application, a BSD should be lightweight while providing adequate assistance during the early trunk flexion following a perturbation. Passive BSDs can be lightweight, but provide limited assistance at small trunk flexion angles, whereas active BSDs can provide adequate early assistance but are typically heavy and bulky. In this study, we evaluated a lightweight (1.97 kg) semi-active BSD to address this tradeoff. The device combines a passive elastic element with an inverse pneumatic artificial muscle (IPAM) that rapidly adds assistive force following perturbation onset. Five healthy participants experienced forward balance perturbations induced by a split-belt treadmill under three conditions: No Device, Passive Mode, and Active Mode. Stability was quantified using whole-body angular momentum (WBAM) and margin of stability (MOS). The Passive Mode did not significantly reduce WBAM RMS or range compared with No Device and significantly decreased minimum MOS. In contrast, the Active Mode significantly reduced both WBAM RMS and range compared with No Device and Passive Mode (all p<0.001) and significantly increased minimum MOS (all p<0.001). These results demonstrate that passive assistance alone may be insufficient for improving stability during forward loss of balance, while rapidly adding active force at perturbation onset can improve balance recovery. The proposed semi-active approach provides the early assistance required for balance recovery while maintaining a lightweight wearable design, demonstrating its potential for improving postural stability.

title: Improving Mapping Capabilities of Soft Growing Robots Through Proprioceptive Sensing
abstract: Soft robots excel at leveraging their compliance to reduce how much impact uncertain external forces have on achieving their goals, increasing robustness and adaptability. Although these deformations are usually treated as passive reactions, these interactions can have rich information about the obstacles and the robot. With proper sensing, one could extract this information and possibly gain more knowledge of the environment through these passive reactions. Soft, growing robots, also known as vine robots are particularly good at passively navigating unknown environments (Hawkes,2017). Their unique locomotion by growth enables them to easily explore cluttered spaces, and previous work has shown that their passive motions could be used to map unknown spaces (Fuentes, 2023). Towards this end, here we demonstrate the use of an inertial measurement unit (IMU) during the deployment of a soft growing robot to extract its movements over time and subsequently reconstruct its environment.

title: Geometric Hoverability Analysis of Generalized Tilted Multirotors
abstract: Generalized multirotors with arbitrarily tilted rotors enlarge the achievable force--moment set, but existing geometric hoverability analyses assume upward-oriented rotors. We decouple the 6-DoF hovering equilibrium into internal moment balance and external force alignment via the Generalized Moment Vector (GMV), which aggregates each rotor's position, tilt, and drag into one descriptor. Under a positive-lift assumption, static hoverability is equivalent to the origin lying in the interior of the convex hull of the GMVs, and reduces exactly to a 2D point-in-polygon test. Inverting the criterion turns center-of-mass (CoM) feasibility into geometry: the GMVs are affine in the CoM coordinates, so rotor-triplet coplanarity conditions yield candidate algebraic boundary curves --- in fact conics --- from which the exact feasible CoM region is recovered by feasibility filtering. Rotor failures reduce to the same criterion on reduced GMV sets, and a geometric margin quantifies the distance of a nominal CoM to the hoverability boundary. Monte Carlo validation on irregular vertical-rotor and tilted-rotor configurations confirms that the filtered algebraic boundary exactly separates hoverable from non-hoverable CoM positions.

title: Universal Robotic Controller (URC): A Wearable Controller for Natural-Motion Teleoperation of Robotic Systems
abstract: The development and adoption of new robotic systems typically requires creating a custom control interface for each platform. This typically adds significant cost, time, and complexity to research and engineering workflows. This project addresses that challenge by developing a single wearable device that can serve as a universal, intuitive control system for any robot operating within the Robot Operating System (ROS) framework. Existing literature and current industry practices indicate a growing interest in intuitive control interfaces for robotics, such as gesture, motion, and electromyographical (EMG) control. However, most control systems are specific to one robot or have limited modularity. The Universal Robotic Controller (URC) seeks to make a unique contribution by developing a platform-agnostic controller that translates a user’s arm, wrist, hand, and finger movements into standardized ROS commands. This approach aims to create a seamless control method for diverse robotic and mechatronic systems, including manipulators, mobile robots, quadrupeds, humanoids, and aerial vehicles, without requiring custom control interfaces for each device. Our group has designed and fabricated the URC V2, a sensor-embedded sleeve equipped with IMUs and pressure sensors to capture fine-grained motion. Future iterations will likely include flex sensors, conductive thread, and dry-electrode EMG to maximize the scope of user intention. Sensor data is processed through onboard microcontrollers, filtered for noise reduction, and mapped and translated into ROS topics representing position, velocity, or gesture-based commands. Our next stage is the development of the universal communication framework. We intend to deploy microROS on the onboard microcontrollers to enable low-latency processing and noise-filtration in the microROS nodes. We also have ROS operating on the Raspberry Pi, which processes and publishes the URC data into the relevant nodes for gesture identification. We will then develop a user-friendly GUI that will allow users to map defined or customized URC gestures into robot action commands. We will test the URC’s compatibility across robot platforms from various OEMs to evaluate accuracy, latency, and ease of use. We expect the URC to provide a unified, time-saving, and adaptable control system capable of real-time, intuitive, teleoperation of any ROS-based robotic project with user-defined controls. With this project, we aim to reduce the developmental overhead and complexity of robotic systems, improve human–robot interactions, and allow users to use a single control system to teleoperate any robotic platform.

title: Development of Remotely Operated Industrial Robotic System using Brain and Muscle Activity
abstract: Most current industrial robotic systems rely on manual controllers, pre-programmed sequences, or stationary teleoperation. These can restrict flexibility and responsiveness within dynamic settings, which can affect productivity and efficiency. Electroencephalography (EEG) and Electromyography (EMG) have been increasingly integrated within the field of robotic control, offering the ability to teleoperate robotic systems using neural and muscular activity. Using biosignals such as EEG and EMG allows implementation of intent-based processing, which can improve factors such as precision, accuracy, and adaptability across a variety of diverse tasks. By combining cognitive decision making with physical activation, this research focuses on integrating EEG and EMG technologies into an industrial robotic platform to enable intuitive, real-time control for additive manufacturing applications. The system uses Steady-State Visually Evoked Potentials (SSVEP) extracted real-time from EEG signals to control a Clearpath Robotics Husky A200 base, while a wearable sleeve with embedded EMG electrodes provides fine-grained control of a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm located on top of the Husky. OpenBCI hardware is used for EEG and EMG signal acquisition, with a custom pipeline developed for processing and classification of biosignals. Reliable EEG and EMG acquisition procedures were established, the proper Robot Operating System (ROS) libraries required for platform control were implemented, and a custom EMG acquisition sleeve was fabricated. By merging cognitive intent, muscular activation, and immersive feedback, this project advances human-robot collaboration and introduces a more adaptive, safe, and intuitive approach to robotic control within industrial settings and beyond.

title: Tactile Stabilization of Unstable Grasp Commands in Vision-Based Dexterous Teleoperation: A Lightweight Two-Layer Correction
abstract: Vision-based teleoperation of multi-finger hands requires no wearable equipment, but hand–object occlusion makes the visual grasp decision unstable: the grasp command flickers, repeatedly opening an established grasp and dropping the object. We present a lightweight two-layer tactile correction: when fingertip GelSight sensors confirm contact, a referencehold layer absorbs transient opening commands, and a perfinger residual regulates noise-normalized contact area while releasing on excessive deformation, without force sensing or learning. On a 16-DoF Allegro hand, the correction substantially improved task success and throughput in a natural four-object task, and reduced object drops six-fold under injected command noise.

title: A Reconfigurable Soft Robotic Leg with Passively Adaptive Flippers for Multi-Environment Locomotion
abstract: Abstract— Robots operating across terrestrial and aquatic environments require appendages with conflicting mechanical characteristics. Ground locomotion benefits from compact structures capable of transmitting concentrated contact forces, whereas aquatic locomotion requires larger interaction surfaces for thrust generation while minimizing drag during recovery.Building on our previous compact terrestrial soft leg and extended aquatic soft leg, this work introduces a modular soft robotic appendage with a deformation-guiding frame and passively adaptive flippers for multi-environment locomotion. The distal structure consists of three articulated carrier modules with silicone flippers that remain expanded during the power stroke and collapse during recovery through passive, direction-dependent mechanical constraints. Preliminary finite element simulations show that guiding the inflation-induced deformation increases the soft-leg tip reaction force from approximately 1 N to 12 N. The resulting architecture combines guided force transmission with passive surface-area adaptation and can be manually configured for terrestrial walking, shallow-water locomotion, and swimming.

title: Energy-Aware Teaming by an Agile Explorer and a Solar-Powered Mothership
abstract: This work presents a cooperative task allocation and path-planning approach for heterogeneous rover teams operating under energy constraints. The team comprises a solar-powered Mothership rover and a battery-limited Jumper rover with complementary capabilities. The key contribution is treating charging-point location as a dynamic optimization variable jointly determined with task sequencing, rather than assuming fixed charging infrastructure. The methodology integrates refined Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT)* for path planning, RRT*-Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) for energy-aware routing, and Genetic Algorithm (GA)combined with PSO for simultaneous optimization of task sequence and charging locations. This mixed continuous-discrete problem is unsuitable for standard Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solvers. Field testing characterized robot performance across varied terrain. Simulation results demonstrate that the multi-rover team successfully completes multi-target missions that neither robot alone can achieve due to energy constraints.

title: Tilt-Dependent DVL Uncertainty: Beam-Aware Covariance for Underwater EKF State Estimation
abstract: Biomimetic underwater robots can rely on a Doppler Velocity Log (DVL) to measure velocity relative to seafloor. They can undergo large body tilts during swimming maneuvers, but the DVL is designed to face downward, with its four acoustic transducers oriented toward the bottom. As the body tilts, its geometry changes, the DVL starts to lose bottom lock, and measurement noise increases. The DVL provides body-frame velocity, a scalar figure of merit (FOM), an onboard 3×3 covariance matrix and raw beam data such as per-beam velocity, range, signal strength, and a validity flag as outputs. Based on test results in a pool, per-beam noise roughly doubles, from 0.0115 m/s at 0–10 degrees to 0.0236 m/s at 60–70 degrees. Also, the sensor's own reported uncertainty is far too optimistic. Both the FOM and the reported covariance do increase with tilt, but they increase differently from the measured noise and their magnitude is off by one to two orders of magnitude across the whole tilt range. The measurement noise covariance (R) tells the filter how much to trust each DVL reading. Since the noise varies with tilt, R should vary with it as well. Four ways of setting R are compared. The first, conventional rejection, applies a constant R below 45 degrees of tilt and skips the update entirely above it. The second and third use the sensor's own reports, fitted against tilt and applied directly: the FOM is a single scalar, so it enters as a covariance scaled by the identity, while the reported 3×3 covariance is used as given. Neither reproduced the measured noise. Under tilt, each beam points in a different direction, so some beams degrade while others do not. The proposed method builds the velocity covariance directly from the four individual beam noise values and their known geometric directions, rather than from one shared number. This lets beams more affected by tilt contribute more uncertainty than beams that are not. The four models were evaluated in a MuJoCo simulation on a dive that ramps to 87 degrees of body tilt and holds, with all models running in the same EKF on identical measurement sequences. Conventional rejection accumulates 2.00 m of position error, and that error does not settle: once the cutoff engages, the estimate is unaided, and drift grows for the rest of the run. Scaling R by the figure of merit gives 0.121 m, and using the reported covariance gives 0.131 m position error; the reported covariance is also the worst of all methods on velocity, at 0.0476 m/s. Beam-geometry R gives the lowest position and velocity error, 0.100 m and 0.0260 m/s, and its position error stays bounded near 0.1 across the maneuver.

title: GeoVPS: A Fast-Slow Framework for Resilient UAV Visual Positioning with Visual-Geometric-Semantic Map Priors
abstract: Long-range unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) navigation requires a persistent geographic reference when Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are unavailable, jammed, or spoofed. Visual-inertial odometry and SLAM provide locally smooth motion but accumulate drift, while map-based metric localization generally assumes an approximate initial position to select the correct map region. We present GeoVPS, a fast-slow visual positioning framework that removes this circular dependency by coupling probabilistic global localization with asynchronous metric 6-DoF pose estimation. A cross-domain representation layer converts UAV imagery, satellite images, and OpenStreetMap data into reusable geographic features. The high-rate fast branch combines compact descriptors with relative motion in a particle filter, preserves multiple position-heading hypotheses, detects loss of map support, and recovers from blind start or localization failure. The lower-rate slow branch evaluates leading hypotheses using dense cross-view registration, corrects scale and yaw mismatch, lifts satellite correspondences to 3D with a digital elevation model, and removes geometrically invalid building matches using semantic map masks before robust PnP estimation. Timestamp-aligned delayed-state fusion integrates accepted map poses without blocking control-rate propagation, while rejected measurements feed back into global-belief recovery. Preliminary real-flight evaluations validate the framework's representation, handoff, and timing contracts across complementary protocols. From a uniform 15 km by 15 km prior, the fast branch converges to the correct geographic region on all 19 blind-start Austin routes, covering 50.7 km and including water-dominated and repetitive scenes. On 20 UAV-Terra3D trajectories spanning 55 km, semantic DEM-PnP localizes 95.69% of frames within 50 m, and delayed fusion achieves 5.88 m mean position error with 100% continuous-localization success within 50 m. TensorRT FP16 descriptor inference requires 3.6 ms on a Jetson Orin Nano Super, while an edge-oriented dense backend requires 130 ms, supporting the intended multi-rate design. These results show that high-rate global belief and lower-rate visual-geometric-semantic registration form a complementary hierarchy for UAVs that must start without a location prior, remain aware of ambiguity, and recover precise map-referenced motion after visual localization degrades. A synchronized end-to-end flight evaluation, including controlled kidnapping and rotational accuracy, remains future work.

title: Bayesian Gaussian Splatting for Uncertainty-Aware Real-Time Manipulation
abstract: Reliable collision avoidance in reconstructed 3D scenes is essential for safe robotic manipulation, particularly under sparse or occluded visual observations. Deterministic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), however, does not explicitly represent reconstruction uncertainty and may become overconfident in poorly observed regions, leading to insufficient collision response during manipulation. We propose BayesGS, an uncertainty-aware 3DGS framework for real-time reactive manipulation. BayesGS models a posterior distribution over Gaussian scene parameters and propagates this uncertainty into occupancy-based safety estimates around the robot body. We then formulate an uncertainty-aware control objective that combines goal-directed motion with scene-dependent collision risk to generate safe end-effector velocity commands. The resulting controller is integrated with a real-time servo loop, enabling the manipulator to react continuously to both occupied and uncertain regions rather than relying solely on deterministic reconstructed geometry. Preliminary real-world experiments with a Kinova manipulator demonstrate the feasibility of uncertainty-aware reactive collision avoidance in sparsely observed and partially occluded scenes.

title: Geometric Sparse Depth Estimation as a Prior for Robot Navigation
abstract: Reliable 3D spatial understanding is essential for autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, and 3D scene reconstruction. Although state-of-the-art depth completion techniques achieve high accuracy, they often depend on heavy foundation models or require explicit sparse 3D measurements. This paper presents a novel, geometrically derived depth estimation method using epipolar transfer with only two monocular images and camera pose estimates. By leveraging known camera motion, the proposed approach synthesizes a virtual stereo pair through epipolar transfer, transforming the two-view temporal correspondence problem into a standard stereo triangulation task while mitigating common geometric degeneracies. The end-to-end pipeline incorporates feature matching, epipolar line computation, virtual frame synthesis, and disparity estimation. We evaluate and validate our method across diverse environments, including outdoor flights with a DJI Mavic Air 2 drone and indoor cluttered scenes within an OptiTrack motion capture facility. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves nearly 90% depth accuracy while maintaining low computational overhead.

title: MABEL: An Open Anthropomorphic Mobile Bimanual Platform for Teleoperation and Learning
abstract: The race toward general-purpose manipulation has produced increasingly capable whole-body robots in industry, but these systems remain largely closed, while open academic platforms typically lack the dexterity, mobility and whole-body articulation needed to capture equally expressive demonstrations. This gap limits both reproducible hardware research and the diversity of data available for learning general-purpose manipulation. We present MABEL, an open anthropomorphic mobile bimanual platform for teleoperation and learning. MABEL combines a three-wheel holonomic swerve base, 0.635,m lift, actuated torso, 3-DOF neck, two 7-DOF arms and two 17-DOF tendon-driven hands, providing 56 functional degrees of freedom at a USD 9,670 bill of materials. Compared with the most articulated open bimanual platform in our survey, MABEL provides $3.5times$ the functional degrees of freedom at $0.69times$ the cost, with a fingertip workspace spanning 0.00 to 2.23,m. CAD, firmware, ROS,2 software and a MuJoCo simulation are released under the MIT license. MABEL supports whole-body teleoperation using an Apple Vision Pro and only head and wrist observations. Analytical retargeting separates head orientation from mobile-base motion without additional body trackers or mode switches, while a compliant whole-body controller incorporates a lift-dependent tip-over constraint. The same controller interface supports teleoperation and learned policies. We demonstrate MABEL on mobile pick-and-place, human handover and long-horizon navigation tasks, providing an open platform for reproducible research in dexterous mobile manipulation.

title: IMPRIMIS: A Novel Wireless Motor Control and Regenerative Braking System for Autonomous Ground Vehicles
abstract: A mobile robot's autonomy stack must be able to send control commands to its motors, yet the high-power electronics create a hostile electrical environment for sensitive computing hardware, which demands a clean separation of high and low power systems. Additionally, software development in the lab should not be coupled to battery drain from the motors - we should be able to run the robot’s computer without needing to give the motors power, and present a reasonable interface to the computer in all cases. We present two subsystems that address both problems: a wirelessly bridged hardware interface that keeps the high and low power domains electrically separate, and a portable power station (PPS) that decouples the robot's computing and sensing from its drive batteries entirely. The PPS generates 120VAC from any one of three sources: wall power, the robot's main LiPO packs, or its own internal battery. In the lab, the robot runs indefinitely from wall power rather than draining battery packs; in the field, the internal battery carries the computer and sensors through a battery swap or power loss, so the autonomy stack never loses power, reboots, or drops its state. The motors and motor driver are powered via a 24V bus generated from a buck-boost converter connected to the main batteries. To account for high reverse-voltage spikes during braking, a regen clamp reroutes back-current into high power heatsinked resistors, dissipating it safely. This protects other sensitive components from damage and ensures a stable voltage on the bus. The link between these two electrical systems is built from a pair of wirelessly-connected ESP32 microcontrollers using the ESP-NOW protocol. This protocol supports ~5ms latency with small data payloads and instantaneous device discovery with known peer MAC addresses. The first ESP board bridges the main PC to all hardware that isn't natively USB or Ethernet enabled, which includes the other ESP board, a radio receiver, and status lights. It streams the desired motor setpoints and operating mode to the other board while relaying measured wheel velocities and other telemetry to the main PC over USB. A switch on the connected radio transmitter selects manual or autonomous mode, but the PC-facing interface and reported telemetry never changes between the two modes. Wheel velocities, active mode, and motor connection status are always reported, so the PC infers the mode purely from telemetry. The second ESP32 manages the motors exclusively and is powered from the motor driver's 5V rail. In autonomous mode, it runs an independent closed-loop PID controller per wheel against received setpoints; in manual mode it applies commanded efforts directly. Wheel encoders are read through this board, and the resulting velocities feed both the PID loops and the telemetry stream. Each board runs its own watchdog and safety checks, so a break at any point in the data stream brings the robot safely to rest.

title: Iris-Actuated Particle Jamming Haptic Display for Lump Rendering
abstract: Palpation training is essential for diagnostic accuracy, yet conventional training phantoms provide limited variability in lump properties and often lack realistic tactile responses. Existing simulators may constrain natural free-hand exploration or rely on pneumatic and hydraulic pumps, reducing portability and increasing system complexity. This work presents a compact, pump-free particle-jamming haptic display that renders palpable lumps with controllable stiffness and size using an adjustable iris mechanism. The iris radially constricts a particle-filled pouch, simultaneously forming a hemispherical protrusion and increasing its stiffness through particle confinement and pouch tension. A six-blade iris module was designed to maintain a near-circular aperture and distribute compression uniformly across its operating range. The device rendered lumps over stiffness and size ranges of 0.3–2.0 N/mm and 8–27 mm, respectively, with increased iris closure producing stiffer lumps and lower iris positions producing larger lumps. The assembled device measured 165 × 166 × 87 mm, weighed 515 g, and required no external fluidic hardware, enabling unobstructed free-hand interaction. A user study with 20 clinicians evaluated 12 conditions comprising three stiffness levels and four sizes. Participants identified stiffness and size with average accuracies of 74.8% and 77.0%, respectively, with negligible correlation between the two measures. These results demonstrate the potential of iris-actuated particle jamming as a compact robotic haptic interface for rendering tunable and perceptually distinguishable lump properties in palpation training.

title: Novel Design of Large-Scale Origami Soft Arm with High Payload
abstract: In modern industrial environments, large-scale rigid robotic manipulators dominate heavy-duty manipulation tasks due to their high structural strength and accurate, well-established control. However, rigid manipulators inevitably suffer from several limitations, including the high system weight, safety risks in human–robot collaboration, and high manufacturing and deployment costs. Soft robotic arms inherently mitigate many of these issues due to their lightweight and compliant structures, but current designs generally exhibit limited payload capacity, restricted workspaces, and poor positioning accuracy under external loads. In this work, we propose a large-scale origami-inspired soft robotic arm that combines a lightweight structure with high payload capacity and sufficient positioning accuracy for practical manipulation tasks. The arm is constructed from modularized layers, each integrating three 3D-printed Yoshimura origami actuators for omnidirectional 3D bending, one 3D-printed Kresling origami structure with an embedded magnetic encoder for self-sensing centerline length, and one IMU for orientation measurement. The robotic arm employs self-proprioception to construct a PCC model of its configuration. In motion control, a multi-step dynamic MPC framework and SLERP trajectory generation is deployed. The proposed approach enables trajectory tracking with an average tracking error of 7.56 mm. Its precision control and high payload capacity provide a viable soft robotic arm solution for future large-scale human–robot collaborative applications. Moreover, its adaptability to varying payloads demonstrates potential for future wearable robotic systems and related applications.

title: ChromaClimber V2: Light-Mediated Controls for a Wall-Climbing Swarm Robotic Platform
abstract: emonstrations for swarm robotics research and public outreach are frequently limited by the cost, fragility, and fabrication complexity of the underlying hardware. Our prior platform, ChromaClimber [1], addressed the space and visi- bility limitations common to ground-based swarm robots by designing a robotic platform that magnetically adheres to and scales a common classroom whiteboard, letting an entire audience observe every robot in a swarm simultaneously, and enabling four light-mediated interaction modalities, spatial programming, shadow instructions, virtual joysticks, and frac- tal plaid GPS localization, two of which (shadow instructions and virtual joysticks) support direct human-to-robot (H2R) interaction. The first iteration, however, was built around fully custom hardware. While this custom design made the platform an effective hands-on training tool, it also required specialized fabrication and assembly skills that limit how easily other labs and classrooms can reproduce or extend the system. This work presents ChromaClimber V2, a redesign of the platform around the Pololu 3pi+ 32U4 OLED (Turtle Edition), a commercially available, fully assembled educational robot kit. Our goal is to determine whether the light-mediated interaction paradigm introduced in [1] can be preserved, and even simplified, on a widely supported, commercial-off-the- shelf (COTS) platform, lowering the barrier for other research groups and classrooms to build on this work.

title: Biomechanical Design, Fabrication, and Reinforcement Learning–Based Control of a 9-DOF Upper-extremity Rehabilitation Exoskeleton
abstract: Upper-extremity rehabilitation robots require accurate multi-joint tracking despite friction, compliance, and parameter error, while maintaining anatomical alignment and bounded actuation. This work presents the design, fabrication, modeling, and real-time control of a modular nine-degree-of-freedom (9-DOF) left-arm exoskeleton spanning five shoulder-complex motions, elbow flexion-extension, forearm pronation-supination, and two wrist motions. A recurrent Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) policy performs state-dependent gain scheduling by generating 27 bounded, joint-specific coefficients for proportional, derivative, and integral-error feedback. The policy was trained with randomized trajectories and dynamics, frozen before deployment, and executed on an NI PXI real-time platform. Against computed-torque control (CTC) under the same nine-joint reference motion and actuator limits, it reduced mean position root-mean-square error from 1.986° to 1.325° (33.3%), worst-joint RMSE from 3.255° to 1.696° (47.9%), and maximum peak error from 5.89° to 2.29° (61.1%). Peak actuator demand was nearly identical (22.44 versus 22.41 N·m), with no saturation. Velocity RMSE increased slightly, so the evidence supports improved position tracking at comparable peak effort rather than universal dynamic superiority. Results are limited to robot-only laboratory testing; human-interaction safety, clinical efficacy, and patient-specific assistance remain to be established.
